section: 5.3 The same name, two different products
text:
5.3 The same name, two different products
The same model is sold differently to a consumer and to an enterprise, and for a B2B firm the difference is the whole game. The consumer tier shares infrastructure, may train future models on your prompts (there is a toggle, check it), rate-limits you, and routes your data through the vendor’s region. The enterprise tier buys data-retention opt-outs, SOC 2 and ISO 27001 compliance paperwork, a region you can pin, and support, at a price that reflects all of it.
For Tessera, handling tenant data, the consumer tier is often a compliance problem waiting to happen. The enterprise tier is where “could we actually deploy this?” becomes “yes, with paperwork.” The two tiers are not the same product wearing different clothes; they are different legal commitments, and treating them as interchangeable is the most common way a promising prototype becomes a breach.

title: 5  What are you giving up?
section: 5.4 Lock-in, and the open-weight escape hatch
text:
5.4 Lock-in, and the open-weight escape hatch
There are two honest arguments for the cloud. It wins on capability (the frontier models live there first) on velocity, because you do no ops, and on integration breadth. The price of all that is control, and the quiet tax is lock-in: your prompt patterns, your agent schemas, your fine-tunes, your evals all grow around one vendor’s API, and leaving gets expensive long before you try. Worse, a vendor can deprecate the model your production system depends on, and you find out in a changelog.
Self-hosting (local or on a VPS, running an open-weight model like Qwen) wins on sovereignty, privacy, deterministic cost, and portability. Open weights mean no vendor can switch your model off from under you; the weights are a file you control. You trade raw capability, and you accept that you operate the thing.
The bet in this book, stated openly, is that a practitioner who has run both makes better procurement decisions than one who has only ever swiped a subscription. That is why you install locally in this chapter.

title: 5  What are you giving up?
section: 5.5 Sovereignty: whose law applies to the prompt?
text:
5.5 Sovereignty: whose law applies to the prompt?
Sovereignty is the legal and geographic question: which jurisdiction’s laws apply to your data while the model is processing it? If your prompt leaves Australia for a US region, it is subject to US law on the way. That is not paranoia. Under the US CLOUD Act (2018), a provider headquartered in or operating through the United States can be compelled by a US warrant to hand over data it holds, even data sitting in a server in Sydney or Frankfurt. An Australian data centre run by a US-based company is not, in legal terms, fully Australian. Following the CLOUD Act’s passage, country after country enacted data-localisation rules to push back.
Local inference sidesteps the question entirely. The data never leaves the device, so there is no transit, no vendor region, no retention policy to audit, and no foreign statute to reach for it. That is the strongest privacy posture available, and it is the one you build in this chapter’s hands-on exercise. The trade (slower, a weaker model than the frontier) is what you “gave up” to get it. Hold both halves.

section: 5.6 You build the local stack
text:
5.6 You build the local stack
This is not a chapter that stays abstract. The stack is three pieces, all on your laptop: Ollama (the engine that runs the model), a model (qwen3:8b, an 8-billion-parameter instruction-tuned model from the same family the shared server runs, sized down to fit your hardware) and Open WebUI, the chat interface you have used since Chapter 1, now pointed at your Ollama.
A detail worth naming: that qwen3:8b tag is already 4-bit quantised, compressed, so a capable model fits into roughly 5 GB and runs on a normal laptop. Quantisation is a chapter of its own later in the book; for now, know that the compression is why this runs on your hardware at all. The price of the compression is some quality, and you will measure exactly how much in the comparison.
When it works, you open http://localhost:3000, pick the model, ask a question, and the answer is computed on your machine. Then you pull the network cable and ask again. It still answers. That is the proof: not a vendor’s assurance, not a compliance tick, but a thing you did and watched survive the loss of the network. Sovereignty, made physical.

title: 5  What are you giving up?
section: 5.7 Three axes, not one winner
text:
5.7 Three axes, not one winner
Now you have both halves on your own desk: the local model you just built, and the frontier model on the shared stack. Run the same prompt on both and the temptation is to ask which is “better.” Resist it. The comparison that matters is along three axes, and a deployment choice is a statement about which axis you are willing to lose on:

Capability: did both answer the question? Where the frontier did better, was the gap material to the task, or just polish?
Speed: how much slower was local? Noticeable, or fine?
Privacy: which answer required the prompt to leave the device?

A frontier model and a local 4-bit model can each produce brilliance and each produce garbage. You are judging outputs, and now also deployments. The capability gap is real, but it is one axis among three, and a deployment that “loses” on capability can be the right call when the other two are non-negotiable.
There is no rule, only a rough decision aid: sensitive or regulated data, low volume, can tolerate a slightly weaker model: local; sensitive data, high volume, needs the frontier: a VPS in a pinned region with a data agreement, open-weight where possible; non-sensitive, speed matters, predictable budget: cloud SaaS. The point is to make the choice consciously, naming the trade, rather than defaulting to whatever the demo used.

title: 5  What are you giving up?
section: 5.8 Inputs and outputs: two different questions
text:
5.8 Inputs and outputs: two different questions
One sharp distinction keeps this chapter honest. The trust tool (average or precise, small or large blast radius) applies to an AI output: the answer the model gives you. The deployment decision is about the input: where your prompt is allowed to travel before it ever reaches the model.
These are separate questions, and a good practitioner answers both. Choosing local protects the input (the prompt never leaves), but it does not relieve you of judging the output: a local model can confabulate a churn signal just as confidently as a frontier one. Conversely, a frontier model on an enterprise tier, properly pinned, can be a defensible home for sensitive data if the output it returns still gets verified. Sovereignty is necessary; it is not sufficient. You still have to prove the thing works.

🌐 Tessera Case
Tessera runs its multi-tenant SaaS on AWS — workload primary region ap-southeast-2 (Sydney), declared standby ap-southeast-1 (Singapore). The data that matters is sensitive: tenant support tickets full of customer detail, billing signals, the contract clauses a churn model reads. Two of Tessera’s internal AI services — an AI summarisation service and a support AI assistant — do their work by calling a third-party model vendor over TLS. That call is the cross-border tension: the vendor’s region is unknown and likely overseas, and it sits outside Tessera’s pinned AWS regions. Pick the churn problem (which tenants are at risk, and why?) and run the deployment decision through it.

For the churn tickets specifically, tenant/customer data sent to the third-party model vendor’s region without a data-processing agreement is a breach waiting to happen, the kind of thing a polished prototype hides and a procurement review catches. Adrian Vasquez, Tessera’s CIO, is right to ask what is buildable, and what is vendor lock-in: the deployment choice is the lock-in question. The honest answer for this data is that the frontier model’s edge on capability is real but non-load-bearing for the task, while the sovereignty cost of sending the data offshore is load-bearing and legal. That is not a brand preference. It is a trade-off, stated and defended.







Note🤖 Conversation Log



Mapping the deployment decision for Tessera’s churn data: with AI, and against it.
I asked a frontier model to recommend cloud, VPS, or local for Tessera’s churn analysis on tenant/customer data. Its first answer was confident and wrong: cloud SaaS, because it offers the best capability. It scored the decision on one axis, capability, and quietly dropped the other two. It had optimised for the demo, exactly the failure mode this book is about.
The correction was the work. I pushed back: tenant/customer data sent to the third-party model vendor’s region without a data-processing agreement is a breach, and the capability edge is non-load-bearing for a summarisation task. The model conceded and revised, but only after I named the constraint it had smoothed over. Left to itself, it would have shipped a compliance problem as a “best practice” recommendation.
Where it was useful: once I held the framing, I used it to draft the sovereignty mapping table above, the mechanical part, the three-by-three grid, the clean phrasing of “what you give up” per row. That is a good use of a thinking partner: it does the typing, I supply the judgement about which trade is acceptable for this data. The deployment decision is mine. The AI’s job was to make the table tidy, not to make the call.








Tip📍 Trust-tool placement



This chapter produces two things, and they sit on different grids.
The deployment decision is about the input: where the prompt may travel. It does not go on the trust tool’s grid at all; it is a separate axis (sovereignty) you answer before you ever produce an output.
The output (say, the local model’s summary of which Tessera tenants are churning, which a retention team will act on) lands squarely in the precise × large quadrant (red). A wrong churn call loses a real customer, and the decision rides on the model’s reading of the data. That means a human signs off before anyone intervenes. Going local protects the input; it does not promote the output out of the red quadrant. Both halves of the decision matter. And both keep mattering after launch; what keeping a deployed system working actually demands is in Appendix D.

section: 5.9 What this leaves open
text:
5.9 What this leaves open
So far we have treated “the data” as if it were a single thing you either protect or send abroad. It is not. Customer data is a layered object: some of it is identifying, some of it is sensitive, some of it can be de-identified and some of it cannot, and some of it, stripped of the obvious names, can still be matched back to a person with enough cross-referencing. Naming where data travels is half the discipline. The other half is knowing whose data it is, what you are allowed to do with it, and what the law says when it goes wrong. That is the next chapter.






Tip🔬 Power-user extension



The Core above — installing Ollama and Open WebUI on your own laptop and watching the local model answer with the network unplugged — is the whole sovereignty argument made physical. Both sides of the trade have a deeper path worth taking once.
On the self-hosting side: do not stop at your laptop. Stand Ollama up on a real box — a desktop with a consumer GPU, or a bare-metal host on-prem — and point Open WebUI at it over the LAN. You now have a Tessera-shaped private inference endpoint that never touches a vendor, and you can put several colleagues on the same model at once: the same “shared floor” argument, at team scale. Measure tokens per second and concurrent users until it breaks, and you have felt the ops cost the VPS row of the table only names.
On the procurement side: take the cloud-SaaS row and turn “data-processing agreement” from a phrase into a one-page checklist — what fields may leave, to which region, under what lawful basis, with what retention, what sub-processor access, what breach-notification window, and what exit/return/deletion looks like. Run it against a real vendor’s DPA. The sovereignty trade stops being abstract the moment you have to sign it.

The US CLOUD Act: Frequently Asked Questions (Cross-Border Data Forum). A clear, authoritative explainer of the 2018 law that lets US law enforcement compel US-based providers to hand over data held abroad, the reason a Sydney server run by a US company is not fully sovereign. Read it to understand the sharpest edge of the sovereignty trade: https://www.crossborderdataforum.org/cloudactfaqs/

5  What are you giving up?

title: 6  Whose data is it?
text:
6.1 The word that misleads everyone
A support engineer at Tessera is drowning in tickets. The instinct (sensible, modern) is to paste the day’s tickets into an AI, joined to the customer record, and let it draft a summary, classify the issue, and suggest a reply for each. Before anyone builds it, someone reassures the team: don’t worry, the customer dataset is anonymised. The names are gone. The emails are gone. So it’s safe, right?
That sentence (the data is anonymised) is the most expensive assumption in applied AI. It is also, almost always, an assertion the speaker cannot defend. This chapter is about why, and about the discipline that turns that assertion into something you can prove.
Two terms travel together and must not. De-identified data has had its identifiers stripped or masked, but the underlying records still exist and can be re-linked. Anonymised data has been transformed so that re-identification is not reasonably possible, by anyone, ever. The first is what most “anonymised” business data actually is. The second is a much higher bar, and it is rarely true of a rich dataset.
The reason it matters is a thirty-year-old result, and it still surprises people. Personally identifiable information (PII) is anything that identifies a specific individual, directly or indirectly, and the indirect part is where nearly all the trouble hides. Direct identifiers (name, email, account number, a face) are the obvious ones. Quasi-identifiers identify nobody on their own, but combined they pin down a single person: postcode plus date of birth plus gender; employer plus job title plus start year; the particular product mix and tenure of one Tessera customer.
In the late 1990s, Latanya Sweeney showed that roughly 87% of the US population is uniquely identifiable from just three quasi-identifiers: postcode, date of birth, and sex. She proved it the memorable way. The governor of Massachusetts had just suffered a heart attack and publicly assured citizens that releasing “anonymised” medical records was harmless. Sweeney bought the voter roll for Cambridge on two floppy disks, linked it to the supposedly anonymous discharge data, and mailed the governor his own health record. The names were gone. The person was not.
“I removed the names” is not anonymisation. It is de-identification wearing a confident label. And AI makes the second look like the first easier than ever, because cross-referencing a “de-identified” set against a public one is exactly the kind of pattern-matching these systems do well. The Netflix Prize dataset, the AOL search-log release, Strava’s heat map exposing military bases: all were “anonymised.” All were re-identified.

title: 6  Whose data is it?
section: 6.2 Where PII hides inside an AI workflow
text:
6.2 Where PII hides inside an AI workflow
An AI pipeline is not one place data lives; it is several, and each is a leak surface:

Training and fine-tuning data. The model memorises and can regurgitate it.
Prompts. Users paste live customer data into a chat box.
Retrieval corpus. A knowledge folder full of tickets, contracts, and emails.
Model outputs. The model echoes back PII it was given or retrieved.
Logs and telemetry. Prompts and responses stored by the platform, sometimes for human review, sometimes indefinitely.

Tessera’s naive ticket-summariser hits all five at once. A production ticket carries a customer name, an account number, and often a screenshot; its free text may name a colleague or quote a contract value. Feed that raw into a summariser and you have placed personal data into every stage above. The risk does not sit in the model. It sits in the flow.

title: 6  Whose data is it?
section: 6.3 What the law says (and why it agrees with the architecture)
text:
6.3 What the law says (and why it agrees with the architecture)
Tessera has offices in Perth, Sydney and Malaga, with a standby region in Singapore, and customers across industries and regions, so it cannot pick one law. Its baseline is the Australian Privacy Act 1988 and its Notifiable Data Breaches (NDB) scheme, administered by the Office of the Australian Information Commissioner (OAIC) — a scheme Tessera knows from the inside, having notified the OAIC of its own TSR-INC-2025-031 breach in early 2025. The operational heart of the Act is the thirteen Australian Privacy Principles (APPs). You do not memorise thirteen. You recognise the four that bite hardest on an AI deployment:

APP 3: collect personal information only for a lawful, necessary purpose. You do not harvest ticket data “in case it’s useful” for a future model.
APP 6: use or disclose it only for the purpose it was collected for. A ticket collected for support cannot quietly train a marketing model.
APP 11: take reasonable steps to protect it, including deletion. Prompts and logs holding PII must be secured and eventually destroyed.
APP 8: you are accountable for personal data sent overseas. Sending customer data to an overseas model server is a cross-border disclosure.

The word reasonable in APP 11 is doing heavy lifting, and it moves with the technology. Pasting live customer PII into a consumer chatbot with no enterprise data agreement is very likely not reasonable. Running the same task on a local model, or on a contracted instance with no train-on-inputs clause, likely is. In October 2024 the Office of the Australian Information Commissioner made that direction explicit, publishing guidance that the APPs apply to every use of AI involving personal information (inputs, outputs, and inferred or hallucinated data alike) and that building a model on personal information is a high-privacy-risk activity. The direction of travel is more obligation, not less.
Then come the stricter cousins. The EU’s General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) is the benchmark the rest of the world measures against, and it is stricter in several load-bearing ways. It requires a lawful basis for every processing activity: there is no default “we can because we have it.” It grants data-subject rights (access, rectification, erasure, portability, objection) that have to be operationally answerable. It makes privacy by design and by default a legal requirement (Article 25), not best practice. It mandates Data Protection Impact Assessments for high-risk processing, which large-scale AI profiling usually is. It reaches extraterritorially: any company offering goods or services to people in the EU is caught, Aus…
California’s CCPA/CPRA, Singapore’s PDPA, and China’s PIPL add their own consent, breach-notification, and cross-border-transfer rules. A global AI deployment hits several at once. The pragmatic response most organisations adopt is the highest-common-denominator approach: build to the strictest applicable standard, usually GDPR, so a single pipeline is defensible everywhere, rather than running five. For a company of Tessera’s size — roughly 210 staff serving around 600 clients — that is usually the only affordable answer.
Notice what survives every framework. Two auditable questions recur, and they map directly onto architecture: where is the data stored and processed, and does that movement across borders trigger disclosure obligations (APP 8, GDPR transfer rules)? And was this data collected for this use, and if an AI use is new, is it compatible with the original purpose? Data sovereignty and purpose limitation carry most of the weight. And the local model from the previous chapter answers the first one by construction: if the data never leaves the machine, there is no cross-border disclosure. That is not a loophole. It is exactly the architectural control the law is asking for.

title: 6  Whose data is it?
section: 6.4 Privacy by design: engineer it in
text:
6.4 Privacy by design: engineer it in
So much for the problem. Privacy by design, Ann Cavoukian’s framing, is the response: privacy engineered in from the start, not bolted on after a breach. Seven principles, condensed: be proactive, not reactive; make privacy the default, so the user does not have to act to be protected; embed privacy into the architecture rather than add it as a feature; pursue full functionality, treating privacy and utility as positive-sum, not a trade-off; protect data end-to-end, including deletion; keep it visible and transparent; and keep the user’s interests central.
For a practitioner, that philosophy becomes a short checklist applied before you build: what data, who needs it, how long is it kept, can we use less, where is it stored, who can read the logs? From that checklist come concrete techniques, and the first two are the ones that actually defeat quasi-identifier re-identification:

Minimisation: send only the fields the task needs. The summariser wants the ticket text; it almost never needs the customer’s email or account number.
Generalisation: coarsen the quasi-identifiers you keep: bin tenure or age into bands, round a location up to a region, band revenue into ranges. This is the control that stops combinations singling out one person.
k-anonymity: after minimising and generalising, each remaining combination of quasi-identifiers should cover at least k records (say, k = 5). If a combination still points at one person, generalise further. k-anonymity is the formal yardstick for “how anonymous is this, really?”
Pseudonymisation: replace identifiers with tokens kept in a separate, access-controlled table, reversible only by a trusted party.
Aggregation: report counts and distributions, not individual rows.
Local routing: run the sensitive step on the local model where data never leaves the machine; use the cloud model only for the non-sensitive step.

Notice the shape of this. The first three controls are the difference between asserting a dataset is anonymous and proving it. “We anonymised the data” is a persuasion; k is a number. That is the spine of this book, applied to privacy: prove, don’t persuade. A vendor’s “we anonymise” is an assertion until you have the k-anonymity figure in front of you.






Note🤖 Conversation Log



Task: audit tessera-customer-data.csv for personal-data risk before feeding the ticket summariser.
Human: “Audit this customer dataset for personal data risk.”
AI (first pass): “No direct identifiers to worry about — no names, emails, or contact details, and Customer_ID is just an internal key. The dataset is anonymised and safe to process.”
Why that was wrong: the AI optimised for reassurance. It checked for the obvious identifiers, dismissed the rest as harmless, and declared safety. “No names” is exactly the false comfort this chapter is about. Stopping there rubber-stamps a re-identifiable dataset as private.
Human (pushing back): “That’s not the question. Customer_ID is an identifier, not a key. For each growing combination of Region → + Industry → + Company_Size → + Primary_Product → + Tenure_Months → + Contract_Value_AUD, count records per bucket and report the smallest bucket — the dataset’s k-anonymity.”
AI (corrected): “You’re right. With 200 customers across 6 Regions and 6 Industries there are only 36 Region × Industry cells, and the distribution is skewed — several hold just one or two customers. Layer on Company_Size (3 bands) and Primary_Product (4 products) and you already have 432 possible cells for 200 rows; add exact Tenure_Months and exact Contract_Value_AUD and almost every remaining combination is unique. Dozens of distinct value-sets map to exactly one customer. k = 1. The dataset is re-identifiable.”
What this taught us about the tool: the AI’s first instinct is to relieve your worry. The practitioner’s job is to convert that relief into evidence. “Looks anonymous” is an assertion; k is a number you can defend.



🌐 Tessera Case · the re-identification hiding in plain sight
Tessera handed over a customer dataset it had “anonymised”, stripping out the company names, contact emails, and account IDs to prove the point. So is it safe?
No. tessera-customer-data.csv has 200 customers spread across 6 Regions (Metro, North, South, East, West, Central) and 6 Industries (Healthcare, Finance, Education, Manufacturing, Technology, Retail). That is only 36 Region × Industry cells before you add anything else — and the distribution is skewed, so several cells already hold a single customer. Layer on Company_Size (3 bands), Primary_Product (4 products), an exact Tenure_Months, and an exact Contract_Value_AUD, and almost every combination collapses to one company. Take one plausible row — Healthcare × Metro × Small × SecureLink × 14 months’ tenure × a precise contract value: that “anonymous” record is a single, named company the moment you cross-reference a public registry, a procurement notice, or LinkedIn. k = 1 across the board.
And notice the two fields everyone assumes are safe. Contract_Value_AUD is an exact dollar figure — match it against a tender database or an invoice and the row is yours, so it is a quasi-identifier in everything but name. Company name is not even a quasi-identifier in disguise; it is a direct identifier that happens to live one join away, in the ticket free text or the CRM note. Neither was stripped, because neither looked like a name.
The redesign applies the controls above before a single record touches a model:

Minimise: drop Customer_ID, any Company name joined in from ticket text, and Renewal_Likelihood. The summariser needs the ticket text and the Primary_Product, not the identity or the churn label.
Generalise: bin Tenure_Months into 1–12 / 13–36 / 37+; band Contract_Value_AUD into ranges (or drop it); collapse Region to a broader territory.
Prove k: re-check after generalisation. If any combination still sits alone in its bucket, generalise further until k ≥ 5.
Pseudonymise: if an identity must travel, replace Customer_ID with an opaque token only the support system can map back.
Route locally: run the PII-bearing step on the local Qwen so data never leaves the machine; send only the de-identified, generalised text to a cloud model, if at all.
Set retention: decide how long prompts and responses are stored and who can read them.

The point is the architecture, not the tool. The same redesign works regardless of which model Tessera picks; that portability is the whole point of privacy by design.







Tip📍 Trust-tool placement



Naive workflow: paste raw tickets, joined to the customer record, into a chatbot to draft a customer-facing reply.

Precise or average? A reply a real customer might receive must be precise.
Blast radius? Personal data spilling into a third party’s logs is large: it cannot be un-leaked.

This lands red: precise, large consequences, and personal data in the flow. A human must sign off, or it does not ship.
Redesigned workflow: minimised fields, generalised quasi-identifiers, k ≥ 5, sensitive step on the local model, identity replaced by a token.
The personal-data blast shrinks, but anything that still emits a response to a real customer does not become green. Well-designed controls move red → yellow: verify the load-bearing bits before sending. A human still reads the suggested reply. The architecture reduces the risk; it does not retire your judgement.

title: 6  Whose data is it?
section: 6.5 Whose data is it, really?
text:
6.5 Whose data is it, really?
Stand back and hear the question behind the chapter. Tessera holds customer data in trust. When an AI workflow touches it, the responsibility does not transfer to the model vendor. It stays with Tessera, and with the engineer who built the flow. The Privacy Act, GDPR, and the trust tool all say the same thing in different registers: the data is the customer’s, held by you, and you answer for where it goes.
This is the last chapter of the Foundation act. You now know what changed, for whom it might fail, whether you can tell, what is in the data, what you give up to deploy it, and, here, whose data it is and who answers for it. The base is built. From here, the work changes. The next act is Build and Prove: you stop reading about AI and start assembling it, the harness that turns a model into a working solution, layer by layer. The first question of that act is the one every working system answers badly or well: are you asking well?






Note🔬 Power-user extension



The Tessera Case asserts k = 1. Prove it. Load tessera-customer-data.csv (Python/pandas, R, or even a spreadsheet pivot) and compute the dataset’s actual k-anonymity: group by Region, Industry, Company_Size, Primary_Product and find the smallest non-empty bucket. Then apply one generalisation pass — bin Tenure_Months into 1–12 / 13–36 / 37+, and drop or band Contract_Value_AUD — and re-measure. Did k rise? To what? That before/after pair is the evidence a privacy review actually wants: not “we anonymised it”, but “generalisation lifted k from 1 to n, and here is the script.”

title: 7  Are you asking well?
text:
7.1 RTCF is the floor you are standing on
You typed the same words your colleague typed. You got the better answer. Naturally you concluded you were the sharper prompter, and you went off to refine your prompts some more.
Hold that conclusion. It is half right, and the half that is wrong is the more interesting half. The gap between your answer and your colleague’s was not (only) the words. It was everything those words travelled through before they reached the model: the standing instructions neither of you wrote down, the documents one of you had attached, the tools one of you had switched on, the model setting one of you had left at default. You have been improving the question and ignoring the room the question is asked in.
By the end of the chapter you will have built both, against Tessera, and you will know which one moved the answer further.
You have used RTCF (Role, Task, Context, Format) in every exercise since Chapter 1. There is no need to recap the four parts here; they are the smallest structure that turns a vague request into a useful one. What matters now is the move that comes after RTCF, because most people stop too early.
Two habits separate a developing prompter from a novice, and neither of them is a cleverer Role.
The first is iterate, don’t restart. Treat the first response as a draft. Push back on it, narrow it, ask for the format you forgot to specify the first time. The second and third prompts in a conversation usually do more work than the first; the model has now seen what you do and do not want, and your follow-up is sharper for it.
The second is verify against the trust tool before you act. RTCF does not exempt a red-quadrant task from human review. A perfectly structured prompt for a task that touches a customer or a contract is still a red-quadrant task. RTCF gets you a competent first response; it does not get you out of the discipline of placing that response on the grid and checking the load-bearing bits. The prompt is a floor, not a ceiling.

title: 7  Are you asking well?
section: 7.2 When one prompt is not enough: chaining
text:
7.2 When one prompt is not enough: chaining
Some jobs are too big, too uncertain, or too consequential for a single prompt. Ask a model to “analyse these support tickets and recommend a strategy” in one shot and it will skim: it has to, because the job contains four jobs and you asked for one. Prompt chaining breaks the work into a sequence where each prompt’s output feeds the next. You have done tiny versions of this without naming it; now name it.
Chaining earns its keep in four ways. It decomposes: asked to first extract themes, then quantify, then recommend, the model goes deeper at each step than it could in a single pass. It verifies at each step: a bad extraction caught at link two never reaches link four. It specialises: each link can carry a different Role and Format tuned to its sub-task. And it routes: an early link can decide which later link to run at all (“is this a billing issue or a technical one?” sends the ticket to different drafters).
Picture a Tessera support chain, four links:

Classify: “Given this ticket, classify it (billing / technical / account / other) and state your confidence.” → a label.
Extract: “List the concrete facts in this ticket (product, error, what was attempted).” → a structured list.
Draft: “Using only these extracted facts, draft a first-response email.” → a draft.
Critique: “Read this draft as the customer. What would make you trust it less?” → a revision list.

Here is the part that matters for this book: each link is small and verifiable, and each link is placed on the trust tool individually. The classification might be green: a wrong label is cheap to catch at the next step. The customer-facing draft is red: it goes to a person before it goes anywhere near a customer. Chaining lets you treat them differently instead of blobbing the whole job into one placement and then trusting all of it or none of it.
Chain when the task has distinct stages that benefit from separate checking, or when a single prompt’s output keeps drifting. Do not chain when the job is genuinely one step; over-chaining adds latency and fresh failure points for no gain. And keep the honest limit in view: a perfect chain on a red-quadrant task still needs a human in the loop. Chaining makes the steps inspectable; it does not make them trustworthy by default.

title: 7  Are you asking well?
section: 7.3 The deeper move: you have been blaming the wrong layer
text:
7.3 The deeper move: you have been blaming the wrong layer
Everything above assumes the words you send travel through a neutral pipe straight to the model. They do not. When you open a chat tool and type a message, you are not talking to a bare model. You are talking to a harness, the wrapper around the model that decides, before your words are ever answered:

what standing instructions (the system prompt) frame every reply,
what context gets attached to your message: retrieved documents, memory, prior turns,
which tools the model can call: search, code execution, file reads,
and which inference engine, which model at which settings, answers.

Change any one of those four and you change the output, without touching the prompt you typed. That is the real reason two people can type the same words and get different answers: their harnesses differ. One has a system prompt telling the model to be terse; the other does not. One has a folder of company documents attached; the other does not. One is on a frontier model at low temperature; the other is on a local model at default. Same words in, different answers out; and the prompt had nothing to do with it.
Think of the harness as four layers stacked around the model:








Layer
What it is
In Open WebUI terms




Prompt
The standing instructions + your message
System prompt + your chat


Retrieval
The documents the model can see
A knowledge / document folder (RAG)


Tool
Capabilities beyond text generation
Functions, web search, file tools


Inference
The model itself + its settings
Model selector, temperature, etc.



The same four pieces exist whether the harness is a consumer chatbot, an enterprise agent, or the local Qwen stack you installed in Chapter 5. Naming them is what lets you design one instead of only ever using one.

title: 7  Are you asking well?
section: 7.4 The demystification: a harness is plain text on disk
text:
7.4 The demystification: a harness is plain text on disk
Here is the move that changes how you see all of this. Every one of those four layers is, at bottom, text and configuration.
The system prompt is a string of text. The retrieved documents are files on disk. A tool description is text telling the model what the tool does. Model selection is a setting. So a harness is a folder of markdown files plus a bit of wiring. That is it. There is no secret sauce.
When you open Pi’s skills folder in this chapter’s exercise, you will see exactly this: directories of markdown. A “skill” is a well-written markdown file in a named folder. You can read it. You can edit it. You can delete it. It is just text, and once you can see the seams, you can change any of them. The “system prompt” you keep hearing about is simply the standing-instructions section of a file like that.
This reframes what you are actually learning to be portable at. The portable skill is designing the markdown files and the folder structure (the system prompt, the knowledge documents, the tool descriptions), not operating any particular tool. Three reasons that matters for a business team:

It travels. Design the folder well and any capable model can use it: Pi, Qwen, Claude, whatever ships next quarter. You are not building a dependency on one vendor’s pricing or survival.
It is auditable. Plain text on disk is something a privacy reviewer, a compliance team, or your future self can actually read. Recall Chapter 6: this is visibility and transparency made literal.
It is teachable without code. You can design, edit, and reason about a harness without writing a line of code. The skill is in the writing, and you already know how to write.

title: 7  Are you asking well?
section: 7.5 You build rough before you are handed finished
text:
7.5 You build rough before you are handed finished
This book teaches the harness across three layers of increasing abstraction, deliberately, so the concept is demystified before it is ever hidden behind a user interface.
Layer 1 (this chapter, in Pi): the harness as raw files on disk. Maximum transparency: you read every instruction the model reads.
Layer 2 (later in this chapter, and in Chapters 5 and 10, in Open WebUI): the same architecture operated through a settings panel: system prompt, document folder, model selector. You control it; the retrieval is partly opaque.
Layer 3 (Chapter 11, NotebookLM): a polished, production-grade harness you did not build. You arrive at it after building the rough version yourself, so the question is not what is this? but what did they build underneath it, and could I build it too?
The ordering is the whole point. You are building, in sequence, the thing you will later be handed finished. Seeing the polished version after constructing the rough one is far more instructive than seeing it first. When a vendor shows you a slick RAG chatbot in Chapter 11, you will not be impressed into silence. You will recognise the seams, because you stitched them yourself.

title: 7  Are you asking well?
section: 7.6 Lands on Tessera: building rough RAG
text:
7.6 Lands on Tessera: building rough RAG
Now the proof. Tessera wants an assistant that can answer questions only Tessera’s own documents would know: what the four core products are, who sits on the leadership team, what each stakeholder wants from an analyst. A bare model cannot know any of that. Ask it cold and it will do one of three things: refuse, guess, or hallucinate with confidence. Ask it cold and you have a trust-tool disaster on your hands: a confident answer to a question the model cannot actually know is the classic red-quadrant trap.
This is where the harness earns its keep, and where you prove it does. The move is small and entirely literal. In Open WebUI you create a knowledge folder, drop in Tessera’s company profile and stakeholder briefs, set a short RTCF-style system prompt (“You are an analyst helping Tessera. Answer using only the attached documents; if the answer isn’t there, say so.”), and ask the same impossible question again. What you have built is retrieval-augmented generation, RAG: the model reads your files before it answers. That is all RAG is, and having wired it with your own hands you will never find it mysterious again.






WarningWatch out: a confident answer is not a sourced answer



The hardest trap in Layer-2 RAG is that a retrieved answer sounds sourced when it is not. The model has read your documents, produced a fluent paragraph, and left you unable to see exactly which chunk of which file it pulled. A precise-sounding answer that grabbed the wrong paragraph is still wrong. The fix is cheap: ask the model to quote the sentence it used. If it cannot, or the quote does not match, you have caught it. Retrieval is a yellow-quadrant output until you verify the source.


Remember the spine of this book. The before-and-after of that impossible question is not a demo to admire; it is evidence. The baseline answer is the assertion. The retrieved answer is the answer with a source you can check. Neither one is “the truth” until you have verified which document the retrieved answer actually came from.
So which lever moved the Tessera answer further toward trustworthy: the rewrite of the words, or the change to the harness? Hold that question. It is the one this chapter’s field journal asks you to answer with a specific change named and a specific move on the trust tool explained. For most people who do this chapter honestly, the answer is the harness, and that answer reframes every chapter that follows.
In the next chapter you stop asking one document at a time and start asking a whole corpus. Tessera has a pile of customer feedback, and the question becomes what is it saying across all of it? The harness idea stays useful: notice how a retrieved document, the move you made this chapter, differs from a pattern found across many documents, the move you are about to make. The folder is still your unit of work. The question just gets bigger.






Note🤖 Conversation Log



Goal. Design the system prompt for Tessera’s RAG assistant, the standing instruction that frames every retrieved answer.
What I asked. I used the model as a drafting partner: “Draft a system prompt for an Open WebUI assistant answering questions about Tessera from an attached document folder.”
Where the AI got it wrong. Its first draft was smooth and plausible, and quietly dangerous. It read: “You are a Tessera expert. Use your knowledge of the company and the attached documents to give comprehensive answers.” That phrase use your knowledge of the company is exactly the trap. It licenses the model to fill gaps from its training, which is precisely what a hallucination needs. A harness that invites the model to confabulate will confabulate, fluently, on every question the folder does not quite cover.
How I corrected it. I struck that clause and rewrote the standing instruction to “You are an analyst helping Tessera. Answer using ONLY the attached documents. If the answer is not in the documents, say so; do not guess.” The model pushed back (“this will make answers terse”); I held the line. The harness, not the prompt, was the load-bearing decision here, and the AI had drafted the wrong harness.
What I decided to trust. The corrected instruction, re-asked against the Tessera folder, correctly refused two questions the documents did not cover and answered three it did. The refusal was the evidence the harness was doing its job.








Tip📍 Trust-tool placement



This chapter produced three outputs, and they sit in three different cells.

The skill markdown file you sketched (Role, standing instructions, format) is green: average is fine, small consequences. It is a draft structure; skim it and move on.
The retrieved Tessera answer is yellow. It needs to be roughly right (precise-ish, sourced), and the blast radius of a wrong product name in a stakeholder briefing is real but recoverable. Verify the load-bearing source (the quoted sentence), and let the rest stand.
The baseline answer from the bare model is red, even though nothing reached a customer. A confident answer to a question the model cannot know is the failure mode this whole book exists to catch. The point of asking it cold is to see the red quadrant, then build the harness that moves the same question to yellow.

The lesson: one chapter, three placements. Never blob a workflow into a single cell.

The artefact: a Tessera knowledge folder (company profile, four stakeholder briefs, a sample support ticket), wired into an Open WebUI assistant with a one-line RTCF system prompt.

What it teaches: RAG is not a product category; it is “the model reads your files before answering.” Having built it from a folder and a sentence of instruction, you can read every other RAG system (vendor demos, NotebookLM, the enterprise chatbot a supplier is pitching Tessera) as the same four layers in a nicer box. That is the demystification, and it is your edge: the supplier’s demo persuades; your before-and-after proves.

title: 8  What is it saying?
text:
8.1 Sorting without being told the piles
Tessera collects feedback the way most growing companies do, faster than anyone reads it. Two hundred customer reviews. A backlog of support tickets with free-text fields full of detail. A quarterly net-promoter score that condenses all of it into a single number, trending gently upward. The dashboard is green. The board is reassured. And nobody, including the board, can actually say what the customers are saying.
This is the chapter’s question, and it is harder than it looks. What is it saying? is not “is it positive or negative?” and not “what’s the average score?” Those are the questions a dashboard answers and a demo performs. The practitioner’s question is the one the dashboard cannot reach: what are these hundreds of voices actually telling us, and where would a tidy number mislead us if we let it?
Two tools do the job, and both are dangerous in the same way: they produce a number that looks like an answer. Clustering finds the themes buried in a wall of text. Sentiment scores the tone. Done honestly, each tells you where to look. Done carelessly, each manufactures a confidence the underlying text does not support. And Tessera, like any company under pressure, will act on the confidence either way.
Picture a librarian facing five hundred returned books. They do not read each one cover to cover. They sort, into a migration pile, a billing pile, a “loves the new dashboard” pile. Clustering is that, automated. An algorithm measures how alike every item is and forms groups, without anyone telling it the group names in advance. This is unsupervised learning: no labels, no right answer to train towards. The machine finds structure. A human decides what the structure means.
For the structured data of Chapter 4 (tenure, spend, region), “alike” was a matter of nearby numbers. For text it is a matter of nearby words. Two reviews are alike if they reach for the same vocabulary in the same proportions. “Sync is slow” and “the sync keeps lagging” land beside each other; “great uptime” lands far away. “Distance,” in this space, is just similarity turned into a number, the smaller the distance, the more alike. (For text the standard measure is cosine distance, and you will choose it from a dropdown, not compute it.)
The grouping itself is almost embarrassingly simple. Tell the algorithm you want k groups; it drops k starting points; every item joins its nearest one; each centre moves to the middle of its new group; repeat until nothing moves. The groups settle because every step only tightens them. That is the whole of k-means. A variant, hierarchical clustering, nests the items into a tree you cut at the level that yields useful themes, so you apply the “how many clusters?” judgement by eye, after you see the groups, instead of committing to it up front.
There is one catch, and it is a human catch, not a mathematical one. The algorithm will give you exactly the k you ask for, even if k is silly. There is no automatic “right” number of clusters. You judge it the way you judge a good paragraph: enough detail to be useful, few enough groups to hold in your head. Five to eight named themes is almost always more useful than thirty micro-clusters or one giant blob.
And here is the move that separates a finding from decoration: a cluster is not an insight until a human names it. “Group 3” tells you nothing. The work, real work, is opening the group, reading the items inside, and writing a one-line label that captures what they share: “billing-cycle confusion among mid-tenure customers.” The algorithm proposes the grouping. You supply the meaning. Skip the naming and you have produced a screenshot, not an insight.

title: 8  What is it saying?
section: 8.2 From words to numbers (without writing any code)
text:
8.2 From words to numbers (without writing any code)
A machine cannot read a review the way you do. Before any of this works, text has to become numbers, and the route it takes quietly shapes everything downstream. The pipeline is the same one Orange’s Text add-on runs for you: tokenise (split into words), lowercase (so Cloud and cloud match), strip the stopwords (the, and, is carry no signal here), normalise (running becomes run), and finally vectorise (turn each document into a list of word-weights, a point in the space the clustering needs).
The choice of vectoriser matters more than it sounds. The simplest, bag of words, just counts how often each word appears. It works, but it over-weights the ubiquitous words and under-weights the rare, distinctive ones that actually define a theme. TF-IDF fixes this: a word earns weight by appearing a lot in one document and in few documents overall. “Sync” turning up in forty of two hundred reviews is distinctive; “service” in a hundred and eighty of them is not. TF-IDF pushes the distinctive words forward, which is exactly what makes clusters separable in the first place.
You will not compute any of this. You will tick a box marked TF-IDF, re-run with it unticked, and the difference between the two cluster maps is the lesson. The preprocessing is not housekeeping; it is where the meaning is either preserved or quietly flattened.

title: 8  What is it saying?
section: 8.3 The sentiment number, and where it lies
text:
8.3 The sentiment number, and where it lies
Once the themes exist, the next reflex is to ask which way they lean. Sentiment analysis takes a piece of text and returns a polarity: positive, negative, or neutral, often with a confidence attached. There are two families, and which one you are holding changes everything.
Lexicon-based scoring (what Orange’s Sentiment widget does) keeps a dictionary of words tagged positive or negative, and the text’s score is simply the net of its words. It is fast, transparent, and needs no training data. Its virtue is also its blindness: it reads words one at a time and has no idea what they are doing together. Model-based scoring trains a classifier on labelled examples. It is smarter about context, but it needs labelled data and arrives in a black box.
Most of the no-code stack, and most of what you will touch first, is the lexicon kind. So attend carefully to what it cannot see, because this is the load-bearing caveat of the whole chapter:

Negation. “Not good” scores as positive, because it contains good.
Sarcasm. “Oh, great, another outage” reads positively to a word-counter.
Domain shift. “Cheap” is a compliment for a bargain and an insult for infrastructure.
Mixed sentiment. “Support is wonderful but the product is broken” has no single polarity, and a single number will average away the very thing that matters.

None of these are exotic. They are the ordinary texture of how unhappy customers actually write. A sentiment score is a coarse signal over many documents, never a verdict on one. Its value lives in the aggregate (“tickets about Analytics Pro and SecureLink skew markedly more negative than the other products”), not in any individual number. Trust the gap between groups; never trust the single score.

title: 8  What is it saying?
section: 8.4 Where Tessera’s feedback actually lands
text:
8.4 Where Tessera’s feedback actually lands
Run the pipeline on tessera-support-data.csv and the clusters name themselves once you read them: a DataVault reliability-and-sovereignty praise cluster, a CloudSync uptime-and-performance praise cluster, an Analytics Pro accuracy-and-reliability complaint cluster, a SecureLink security-and-connectivity complaint cluster, a billing-cycle confusion cluster among the mid-tenure customers. Switch the tickets to sentiment and group by product, then by region, and a pattern surfaces that no single review would have shown you: Analytics Pro and SecureLink skew most negative (Analytics Pro a mean rating near 2.1, SecureLink near 2.5), while CloudSync (~4.1) and DataVault (~4.2) are the happy products, and the gap is sharpest in the South and Metro territories. The follow-up rate tells the same story: roughly three in four Analytics Pro tickets and two in three SecureLink tickets need a follow-up, against barely one in ten for DataVault and CloudSync.
That is a finding. “Customers complain about Analytics Pro and SecureLink” is a vibe; “Analytics Pro and SecureLink skew more negative than the rest of the portfolio, and most sharply in the South and Metro territories” is something a product decision could rest on. The clustering did the finding. You did the naming. Neither is ground truth; both are starting points that tell a human where to look.
And notice what this finding is not standing on: one method, one time. Tessera’s churn model in Chapter 4 surfaced the same two products — Analytics Pro and SecureLink — as the ones customers leave. Two independent methods, different data, same problem products. That convergence is cross-validation, and it is the kind of agreement that earns trust: not because either analysis is perfect, but because each corroborates the other without being designed to.
Now hold the tension the chapter is built to teach. The same analysis that surfaced a real pattern also handed you a sentiment number that is, in the lexicon’s hands, partly fictional. Re-score the same Analytics Pro and SecureLink tickets with a second, model-based scorer and join the two columns side by side. Filter to the disagreements. Read eight or ten of them. Those tickets (the sarcastic “love paying for outages”, the negated “not happy with Analytics Pro”, the infrastructure “cheap” the lexicon read as praise) are exactly where the scorer silently failed. The size of that disagreement is your evidence for how far a single sentiment number can be trusted in a Tessera decision. Most of the time, the answer is: not far enough to act on alone.

🌐 Tessera Case
The artefact is not the cluster screenshot. It is two things together: the named theme maps (DataVault and CloudSync praise — reliability and sovereignty; Analytics Pro and SecureLink complaint clusters — accuracy and connectivity) and the disagreement set, the same Analytics Pro and SecureLink tickets re-scored lexicon-then-model, filtered to where the two scorers part ways, with eight to ten of those tickets read in full. The headline finding is “Analytics Pro and SecureLink skew most negative in the portfolio, sharpest in the South and Metro territories.” But the defensible artefact, the thing a consultant report can actually stand behind, is the disagreement set, because it is the evidence that a single sentiment number is not enough to act on. The screenshot persuades; the disagreement set proves.

title: 8  What is it saying?
section: 8.5 The number is not the decision
text:
8.5 The number is not the decision
This is where the discipline of the book bites. The theme is a summary, so it leans average, and on the trust tool, average usually points towards green. But the decision the theme feeds is a different animal. A finding that justifies sunsetting Analytics Pro or SecureLink in a region is not data analysis you can skim. The model did not make that decision; a human leaning on an un-checked aggregate will. Name the blast radius before you name the recommendation.






Tip📍 Trust-tool placement



Where does the Analytics Pro and SecureLink sentiment gap sit? The theme itself is a summary, so it leans average, but the decision it feeds (resource allocation, a region’s product roadmap) has a large blast radius. That lands it at 🟡 yellow, sliding towards 🔴 red: verify the load-bearing claim before anyone acts on it. Concretely, that means reading the raw South and Metro tickets behind the gap, and confirming the lexicon score against a second scorer on the disagreements. The output looks like “safe data analysis” right up until it justifies sunsetting a product in a region, then it is a red-quadrant decision wearing a green-quadrant costume. The placement, not the widget, is what fails.








Note🤖 Conversation Log



You sanity-check a cluster label with the shared AI stack, using the RTCF prompt frame. You feed the model eight Analytics Pro tickets and ask for a one-line label. It returns “Analytics Pro pricing and value complaints.” Plausible, except that when you read the eight tickets yourself, four of them are not about price at all; they are about reporting accuracy dressed up in the language of cost (“paying through the nose for dashboards that lie daily”). The model collapsed two distinct grievances, accuracy and value, into the more marketable one. You relabel the cluster “Analytics Pro accuracy-and-reliability complaints, with cost as a proxy for frustration” and split it.
In the same session you ask the model to score the sarcasm in “love paying for outages.” It flags it correctly as negative, where the lexicon scorer had read it positive. The lesson is not that the AI is wrong, nor that it is right. It is that it is both in the same sitting, and only the human reading decides which is which. The model proposed a tidy label; you supplied the distinction that mattered. That correction (written down, with the tickets that forced it) is exactly what your conversation log entry is for.








WarningWatch out: it’s just data analysis, it’s safe



No, it is not. A sentiment finding that justifies sunsetting a product in a region is a red-quadrant output even though it came out of a harmless-looking Orange widget. The model did not make the decision, but a human leaning on an un-checked aggregate will. The danger is never the tool; it is the confidence the tidy number lends to the recommendation.

title: 8  What is it saying?
section: 8.6 What this chapter proved, and what it didn’t
text:
8.6 What this chapter proved, and what it didn’t
What text mining gave Tessera is genuine: themes a human would have taken a week to surface, and a sentiment gap sharp enough to act on. What it did not give is certainty. The clusters needed naming, the sentiment number needed a second scorer to check it, and the headline finding needed a human to read the raw tickets before anyone touched a product roadmap. That is not a failure of the tools. It is what the tools are for: accelerating the looking, not replacing the judging.
The sentiment number lied to you in predictable, nameable ways, and you caught it because you went looking for the lie. That habit (expect the failure, measure it, name its size) is the whole posture the next chapter formalises. “Does it actually work?” stops being a question you ask of one output and becomes a discipline you apply to the whole solution: a threshold stated up front, an honest measurement against it, and a record of who it fails. The cluster map and the sentiment gap were the easy part. Proving the thing works is what earns this book its title.






Tip🔬 Power-user extension



The Core path — Corpus → Preprocess Text → TF-IDF → Distances → Hierarchical Clustering, then Sentiment grouped by product and region — is complete and correct on its own. To push further, add the second scorer: train a model-based sentiment classifier (Orange’s Logistic Regression or SVM on a small hand-labelled slice of tickets), score the same documents, and join it beside the lexicon column. Now the work is the disagreement set — filter to where the two scorers part ways, read the tickets, and quantify the error: what share of Analytics Pro tickets does the lexicon mis-score, and is that share the same for SecureLink? Compute the worst-group error — which product’s sentiment is least reliable — and put that number in the report. A sentiment finding that names its own weakest group is the difference between a number and an honest number.

title: 9  Does it actually work?
text:
9.1 The demo and the deployment are different objects
You have just trained a neural network in a browser. No code. You pointed your laptop’s camera at a Tessera home router, captured twenty photographs of its status LED glowing green, twenty glowing amber, twenty pulsing red, clicked Train Model, and watched a machine learn in seconds. You exported it, pasted one URL into a Glitch starter, and now it is live on your phone. A customer points their camera at a router and your app says healthy or fault.
It works. In the room, on your laptop, under the lights you trained on, with your hand holding the phone, it works every time. If this were a vendor pitch, you would stop here, applaud, and ship.
This is the moment the book has been building toward, and the question that stops you is the book’s own title: does it actually work? Everything in this chapter (arguably the whole discipline of applied AI) turns on refusing to confuse the demo you just made with the deployment Tessera would rely on.
A working demo proves one thing: the solution runs. It says nothing about whether Tessera should rely on it, and reliance is the only question that matters once a model touches a customer. The gap between runs and reliable is where applied AI actually lives, and it is not a gap you close with a more impressive model. You close it by evaluating: stating what good enough means, measuring against it honestly, and naming where it fails.
That sounds plain. It is meant to. The most expensive failure mode in applied AI is not a buggy model; it is a slick model that nobody ever bothered to break. Evaluation is the discipline of breaking it on purpose, before a real user, or a real adversary, does it for you.

title: 9  Does it actually work?
section: 9.2 Three lenses, not one number
text:
9.2 Three lenses, not one number
When you ask “does it work?”, the first answer people reach for is accuracy: it got 90% right. Accuracy is the obvious lens, and it is the one people stop at, which is exactly why it misleads. Headline accuracy is an assertion, not evidence. The question that turns it into evidence is 90% on which class, at what cost to the others?
A router-status classifier that is 90% accurate overall but misses seven in ten faults is useless for triage, because the fault class is the only one that matters and it is the one being sacrificed to keep the headline up. Look at the class that matters, not the headline. Measure per class, always.
Accuracy alone never settles “does it work?” A working evaluation holds the solution up to three lenses:

Accuracy: how often is it right, per class, measured on data it has never seen?
Fairness: does it work equally across the groups it serves? The same model can be accurate overall and quietly wrong for a subgroup: a lighting condition, a region, a hand that is not yours.
Explainability: could you tell Tessera’s CEO, Henrik Larsson, why it flagged this customer, in words a non-technical person would accept? “The model says so” is not an answer; it is the cap on how much anyone should trust it.

The three lenses are not a checklist to tick. They are three different questions that a single number (accuracy) pretends to answer all at once. Read them as a demand: prove it works on the class that matters, for the people it could fail, in a way you can defend.






WarningWatch out: the headline is a hiding place



“90% accurate” is the phrase that lets a solution look finished when it isn’t. Overall accuracy is a weighted average, and averages hide the people (and the classes) the model fails. A churn model 90% accurate overall that misses 70% of actual churners is useless for retention; the headline never tells you. The cure is mechanical: never report an overall number without the per-class and per-group breakdown beneath it.

title: 9  Does it actually work?
section: 9.3 “Good enough” is a judgement, not a number
text:
9.3 “Good enough” is a judgement, not a number
Here is the idea that turns evaluation from arithmetic into judgement: the same model can be fine in one place and dangerous in another, at exactly the same accuracy. Fitness for purpose is set by the decision the solution feeds, and the threshold is set by the blast radius of being wrong.
If your router classifier mis-routes a healthy ticket to the wrong queue, a human glances at it and moves it along. Small blast radius; an average solution is tolerable. But if it silently calls a fault healthy, an angry customer waits while their router stays down. That is a large, hard-to-reverse blast radius, and the same 80%-accurate model that was fine for the first job is dangerous for the second.
This is the trust tool from the Introduction in another form. Small blast radius tolerates an average solution; large blast radius demands precision and a human in the loop. So before you measure anything, you write one sentence: “For [decision], good enough means [threshold], because [blast radius].” A model without a stated threshold is a demo, not an evaluation. The threshold is the thing you measure against, and the thing you cannot quietly move after the fact to make a weak result look strong.

title: 9  Does it actually work?
section: 9.4 Test to destruction
text:
9.4 Test to destruction
Most testing asks “does it work on normal inputs?” Adversarial testing asks the opposite: what inputs make it fail? You are not being cruel to your model. You are finding its edges before a real user does.
Every solution has a failure surface. The light is dim. The hand is shaky. The background is a carpet instead of a desk. A customer photographs the router in a dark cupboard at midnight, because that is when the fault showed up. A demo evaluated only on the happy path has proven nothing about the conditions that will actually bite.
Adversarial testing is a posture, not a technique: take every assumption your model is making and feed it the opposite. For a vision classifier, that is lighting, angle, distance, background, a photograph of nothing at all. For a churn model, it is a customer with missing fields, or one sitting right on the decision boundary where flipping a single input flips the prediction. For a RAG setup, it is a question the documents don’t answer, and watching whether it admits ignorance or invents a confident lie.
Then there is VET, a three-move self-adversarial check you run on your own outputs, borrowed from the companion book:

Verify. Re-derive the load-bearing claim independently. Asking the model “is this right?” is not verification; the thing that produced the answer cannot be the thing that confirms it. Check it against the data, the source documents, a photograph it has never seen.
Expose. Name what would have to be true for the output to be wrong, and who it could fail. This is the fairness lens, made personal: you are stating your assumptions out loud before the model breaks them for you.
Test. Feed it the cases most likely to break it. The ones that fail go straight into your report.

VET is the discipline that stops you rubber-stamping your own work. It is the trust tool as an action, not a label: verify the claim, expose the assumption, test to destruction.

title: 9  Does it actually work?
section: 9.5 The honest report
text:
9.5 The honest report
Here is the part that feels counter-intuitive and is, in fact, the point. A report that says “82% overall, but only 61% under dim light, below our 80% threshold on the only class that matters” is a stronger report than one that claims the model works. Finding a real failure, naming it, and saying what a human must do about it is worth more than a flawless demo.
This is not a consolation prize for a model that under-performed. It is the integrity gate. A report that only shows successes has told the reader nothing useful, because every demo can be made to succeed on its own training data. The thing a business cannot buy from a vendor’s deck is the honest map of where the solution breaks, and that map is the practitioner’s actual deliverable. Prove, don’t persuade stops being a slogan the moment you write down a threshold your solution misses and ship the report anyway.






Note🤖 Conversation Log



Evaluating the shipped router classifier, you ask an AI assistant to draft the assessment. You feed it the results. It returns: “The model performs well and is ready for deployment: 85% overall accuracy across all classes.”
That is the moment to push back, because the AI has done what AIs do: it read the headline and composed a confident conclusion. You reply: “Show me per-class, then per condition. Overall accuracy is not the deliverable.” It produces the breakdown: healthy 94%, degraded 80%, fault 38%. The fault class, the one with the large blast radius, is where the model collapses, and the headline hid it completely.
Then you ask the question the AI did not think to ask: “And under dim light?” Fault drops to 0%. The AI’s first draft (“ready to deploy”) would have shipped a red-quadrant failure as a green-quadrant success. The correction was not a flourish; it was the refusal to accept an average, the demand for the per-class and then the per-condition view, and the willingness to keep pulling until the model broke. That challenge, logged unedited, is the integrity gate, and it is also what separates a defensible evaluation from a rubber-stamped one.

title: 9  Does it actually work?
section: 9.6 What the measurement earned
text:
9.6 What the measurement earned
You now know enough to place the model, and the placement is not a label you choose, it is a consequence of what you measured. This is the trust tool doing its real work: turning evidence into a decision about how much human oversight the deployment needs.






Tip📍 Trust-tool placement



The router classifier feeds two different decisions, and they sit on different squares of the grid.

Routing a healthy or degraded ticket: average is fine, blast radius is small (a wrong route costs a human a glance): 🟢 green, light review, the model can triage on its own.
Clearing a fault: must be precise (catch every fault), blast radius is large (a missed fault leaves a customer offline): 🔴 red, human-in-the-loop, non-negotiable.

The honest placement is therefore split: green for triage, red for fault confirmation. And because your measurement showed the model fails exactly on the red-quadrant class (0% on faults under dim light), the placement is earned, not assumed. You did not decide to keep a human in the loop on faults because it felt responsible; you decided because the evidence demanded it. A model that quietly creeps up to 99% next year could move that red square to yellow, but only if a future evaluation proves it, per class, under the conditions that broke it this time.



🌐 Tessera Case
The router-status classifier, evaluated to destruction. You trained the model in Teachable Machine on twenty photographs per class (green (healthy), amber (degraded), red (fault)), varying angle and background on purpose, exported it as TensorFlow.js, and shipped it to a live Glitch web app a customer can open on their phone.
In the room it was untouchable: 96% accurate. Then you held back five photographs per class that the model had never seen, and ran all three lenses. Accuracy, per class: healthy 94%, degraded 80%, fault 38%, the headline still read 85%, the arithmetic of an imbalanced reality. Fairness, sliced by condition: under dim light the fault class fell to 0%. The model called a red LED healthy because it had never trained on a dim red, and customers photograph faults at midnight, in cupboards, exactly when the light is worst. Explainability: a neural net is a black box; you could not tell the CEO why it said healthy, only that it did, and on the fault class that limit is not acceptable.
The finding is the gap: 0% on the one class with the large blast radius, hidden behind an 85% headline. The decision, written into the report: ship it for triage routing, with a human confirming every fault the model clears, until the training data covers the conditions that broke it. That is not a failed prototype. It is an evaluated one, and it is the only kind Tessera should ever rely on. What it takes to run an evaluated prototype live, with oversight that survives real volume, is the subject of Appendix D.

title: 9  Does it actually work?
section: 9.7 From one model to the whole job
text:
9.7 From one model to the whole job
There is a reason this chapter is the title of the book. Every other question (what changed? for whom? can you tell?) funnels toward this one, because “does it actually work?” is where the demo meets its evidence and the practitioner earns the moat. A single model, evaluated honestly across three lenses, tested to destruction, and reported with its failures intact, is tractable. You can hold it in your head, place it on the grid, and defend the decision.
But Tessera does not want a classifier. It wants an agent that reads the incoming ticket, fetches the customer’s history, classifies the photograph, drafts the response, and decides whether to escalate, a chain of outputs, each with its own failure surface, each needing its own threshold and its own placement on the grid. The moment you hand the model tools and let it act, the question stops being “does this model work?” and becomes the next chapter’s: can it do the whole job, and how much of that job can you safely hand over? That is where the red quadrant gets genuinely dangerous, and where the evaluation discipline you just learned becomes the only thing standing between a working system and a catastrophe that looked, in the demo, like magic.






Tip🔬 Power-user extension



The Core above — train in Teachable Machine, export to TensorFlow.js, ship a Glitch live app — is the complete, no-code path, and doing only that is correct. If you want to go deeper, two optional directions:

Self-host the model. Export the model.json and weight-shard .bin files and serve them from your own Glitch project, a static host, or a small server you control, instead of hot-linking Teachable Machine’s bucket. You now own the artefact end to end — its uptime, its version, and its data residency — which is exactly the cloud-versus-self-hosted tension a Tessera deployment has to settle.
Run a systematic fairness audit. Build a held-out test set split deliberately across the conditions that could break the model — dim light, off-angle, phone-shake, a carpet background, a different hand behind the camera. Compute accuracy per condition and per group. Then quantify the worst-group gap: the largest spread between your best and worst condition. That single number is the honest headline. If it is large, no overall accuracy rescues you — and you have just produced the per-group breakdown the three-lens measurement demands.

These are depth, not the real version. The Core is complete on its own.

title: 10  Can it do the whole job?
text:
10.1 From answering to acting
Every system you have built so far in this book has been a responder. You asked; it answered. A classifier sorted a row. A RAG chatbot pulled a paragraph. A sentiment model labelled a ticket. In every case the human decided what to do with the output. The model produced text; you produced action. That line is the entire safety model of chapters one through nine.
An agent erases the line. An agent is a model wired to tools and a loop, and the loop is the whole difference between “answer my question” and “do this job.” The model has not changed, it is still doing next-token prediction, still the same Qwen you pointed at a document folder in chapter seven. What changes is the harness around it. Instead of answering once, the harness lets the model run a cycle:
That loop is seductive. It is also where every agentic failure you have ever read about was born. The airline chatbot that promised a customer a refund the airline never authorised did not fail because the model was malicious. It failed because the model was inside a loop that let it act (send a message, file a record) on the strength of its own confidence. The blast radius moved from text on a screen to a commitment a company had to honour.
This chapter is not a warning against agents. It is the opposite: it is how you build one small enough to understand, and then (the actual skill) decide where the human stands inside its loop before you switch it on.

section: 10.2 The blast radius lives in the tools, not the model
text:
10.2 The blast radius lives in the tools, not the model
The single most useful idea in agentic AI is this: a tool call is structured output, not a paragraph. When the model decides to act, it does not reach into your file system. It emits something that looks like a function call (search_docs("churn", region="Metro")) and the harness executes it, handing the result back. The model proposes; the harness disposes.
This matters because it tells you exactly where the danger is. A read-only search is low risk: the worst it does is return a slightly-off document. A tool that sends an email, files a support ticket, refunds a payment, or closes an account is high risk, because those actions touch people, money, and records you cannot walk back. You do not control the danger by hoping the model is careful. You control it by controlling which tools the harness exposes, and, just as importantly, by reading every exposed tool as a permission you have granted the loop.
A vendor will tell you their agent is “safe” because the model is aligned. That is persuasion, not proof. The proof is the tool list: what, precisely, have you let this loop do? That list is your risk register. If you cannot name every action the agent can take, you have not evaluated it.

text:
10.3 MCP: a standard plug for tools
Wiring tools to a model used to be bespoke work: one integration per tool, per model, per harness. Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard that replaces the tower of custom plumbing with one shared interface. The analogy the spec itself uses is apt: MCP is the USB standard, but for AI tools. Write a tool once as an MCP server, and any MCP-aware model and harness can call it.
You will not build an MCP server this chapter, and you do not need to. What you need is to recognise it when a vendor mentions it, because “the agent reached into our CRM” stops being a custom build and becomes a standard pattern the moment MCP is involved. That is convenient. It is also why the tool-list question gets harder, not easier: a standard plug means a standard way to hand the loop a dangerous capability. The convenience and the risk are the same feature.
