section: 10.4 Skills folders: an organisation of agents, in text
text:
10.4 Skills folders: an organisation of agents, in text
Here is this book’s central agentic idea, and it is simpler and stranger than it sounds. In chapter seven you opened the skills folder and saw markdown files and folders. Extend that one step and you have an agent that spawns sub-agents with no infrastructure at all:

A skill file is an instruction set for one specialised job: “you are the churn-analysis sub-agent; read the customer data, return the top three risk signals, do not speculate beyond the data.”
The main agent reads the skills folder, picks the skill that matches its next step, and dispatches the sub-task, sometimes to itself with a new instruction, sometimes to a fresh model call.
That is a single agent spawning specialised sub-agents on demand, using nothing but folders and text.

No orchestration framework. No new infrastructure. The harness you already understand is doing the work. This is Layer 2 of the harness (the prompt layer) extended to carry an organisation. And the insight that travels is this: you design an agent’s skills folder the way you design a team. The division of labour is the design decision. A ticket-clusterer, a knowledge-searcher, a brief-drafter: three sub-agents, three skill files, one coherent workflow. Get the division wrong and the whole loop drifts; get it right and any capable model can run it.
RAG moves inside the loop at the same moment. In chapter seven you built retrieval by pointing the model at a document folder and letting it answer. In an agent, retrieval becomes one tool among several: the agent retrieves from the Tessera folder as a step in its loop, then reasons over what it found, then acts. Grounding each action in a real document is precisely what stops the agent inventing a plausible-sounding but wrong internal fact halfway through the workflow. It is also, as you are about to see, the thing that fails first.

section: 10.5 The danger zone
text:
10.5 The danger zone
Now pull up the trust tool you have carried since the introduction. Ask the two questions of an agent’s output, before you act on it:

Does it need to be precise, or is average fine?
If it is wrong, how big is the blast radius, small or large?

An agent that takes actions almost always lands in the same cell. It must be precise: it is filing, sending, classifying, recommending, and a “pretty good” action that is wrong is still wrong. And its blast radius is large: actions touch people, money, records, and decisions you cannot easily walk back. That bottom-right cell, precise and large, is the danger zone, and it is the natural home of agentic AI.
This is not an argument against agents. It is an argument for designing the human in before you switch the loop on. Because here is the thing about a loop: drift compounds. Each step the agent takes builds on the last. A slightly-off retrieval in step two becomes a confidently-wrong theme in step three becomes a brief to the COO in step four that is built on a fact nobody ever checked. By the time a human glances at the finished output, several steps of drift have already been baked in, and the human is approving a fait accompli, not making a decision.

section: 10.6 What “human-in-the-loop” actually means
text:
10.6 What “human-in-the-loop” actually means
It is not “a human glances at the end.” That is a rubber stamp wearing a safety vest. Human-in-the-loop is a checkpoint you design into the workflow so that a human makes the load-bearing decision at the load-bearing moment. Four common patterns, in increasing autonomy:

Approval gate. The agent drafts; a human approves before any action fires. Safest, slowest.
Review checkpoint. The agent runs freely within a sandbox, but must stop and surface its work at a defined point for human review.
Confidence threshold. The agent acts on its own when its confidence is high; escalates to a human when it is not. Requires the model to know when it is unsure: use carefully, and never as your only safeguard.
Dry-run then execute. The agent produces a plan of actions; a human reviews the plan; only then does execution proceed.

The skill is not picking the most autonomous pattern. The skill is matching the pattern to the blast radius, and, harder, placing the checkpoint at the right step. The wrong place is “at the very end, after everything is done.” The useful question is the one you should tattoo on this chapter:

At which step does the output become load-bearing or irreversible?

Put the checkpoint just before that step. Everything before it can run fast and cheap. Everything after it carries a human’s decision forward, and you can defend why you put it there, and not one step later. That defence is the actual deliverable. “Put a human here” is easy. Justifying why here and not one step on is the practitioner’s edge.

section: 10.7 The provocation
text:
10.7 The provocation
Here is the question the whole book keeps circling, and this chapter it lands hardest:

If the loop runs without you (drafts, retrieves, decides, acts) what exactly is your role, and is that role stable?

A defensible answer is not “I review everything.” That is the Delegation Trap from chapter three, now at workflow scale: rubber-stamping every output until the stamp loses its meaning, at which point you are not in the loop, you are blocking it, and the pressure to remove you will be enormous. A defensible answer sounds more like this: I design the checkpoints, I own which tools the agent can call, I decide which outputs are red-quadrant, and I can explain why the agent did what it did. Notice how much of that is design and judgement, not keystrokes. The work that survives automation is upstream of the loop: choosing the tools, drawing the boundaries, naming what must not run unattended.
You do not need a final answer this chapter. You need to notice the question, and you will record it in your working log, because it is one of the book’s secondary threads.






Note🤖 Conversation Log



Building the Tessera support digest, the agent drifted, and the conversation log is where it got caught.
Goal. Have the agent read the week’s new support tickets, find the top three themes, check the internal knowledge folder for a relevant answer to each, and draft a short brief for the COO.
Where the AI got it right. It cleanly split the job into three sub-agents (a ticket-clusterer, a knowledge-searcher, a brief-drafter) and dispatched them in order. The skills-folder design was sound.
Where the AI got it wrong. The knowledge-searcher sub-agent, asked to find an answer to a theme about “intermittent latency on Premium routes,” returned a confident paragraph that sounded like it came from the runbook. It had not. No retrieval had fired on that step; the sub-agent had drafted from its parametric memory instead of from the Tessera folder, and it did not flag the difference. The brief-drafter then built a recommendation on top of the invented fact. Two steps of compounding drift, invisible in the final prose.
The human correction. The checkpoint was placed between search and draft: every knowledge-searcher claim had to cite the document it was retrieved from, and the reviewer checked one citation at random before the drafter was allowed to proceed. The invented fact failed the citation check and was caught. The lesson, written into the log: grounding is not a property of the model; it is a property of the tool call, and an agent that could retrieve but didn’t looks identical to one that did. Verify the retrieval, not just the prose.
What was trusted: the clustering, after a spot-check. What was refused: the recommendation, until the citation was real.








Tip📍 Trust-tool placement



The agent’s brief to the COO lands red: precise, large blast radius. A leader may act on it; it is drawn from real customer tickets; getting a theme wrong wastes a week of the customer-success team’s attention, and getting a recommendation wrong routes engineers at the wrong fault. Red means a human signs off, and the sign-off has to be Real, meaning the human checked the load-bearing bit (here, the citations behind each recommendation), not just skimmed the prose.
The agent’s intermediate steps live elsewhere on the grid: the ticket clustering is yellow (verify the load-bearing bit: did it miss a whole segment?), the raw retrieval is green (skim and use, it is just a document pull). Trust-tool placement is not one decision per agent; it is a decision per step, and the red steps are where your checkpoint goes.



🌐 Tessera Case
Grace Sullivan, Tessera’s COO, wants a weekly digest she can act on: read the new support tickets, find the top three themes, check the internal knowledge folder for a relevant answer to each, and draft a short brief. Your team builds it as a multi-step agent.
The skills folder carries three sub-agents (a ticket-clusterer, a knowledge-searcher, a brief-drafter) and the main agent runs the plan-retrieve-draft-assemble loop against the Tessera document folder as its RAG tool. It works. It is impressive in the demo. It is also red-quadrant the moment the brief is destined for someone who might act on it.
The design decision that earns the engagement is not the agent. It is the checkpoint: between search and draft. Every claim the knowledge-searcher returns must cite the document it was retrieved from; a human checks one citation before the drafter is allowed to proceed. Everything upstream (clustering, retrieval) runs fast and cheap. Everything downstream carries a reviewer’s decision forward.
What breaks if the checkpoint is removed. Remove it and the loop runs end to end unattended. Drift compounds across the steps: an unretrieved “fact” in the search step becomes a confident theme in the draft becomes a recommendation a leader acts on. The first time nobody notices is the time the brief is wrong in exactly the way the model is most persuasive: fluent, structured, and ungrounded. The agent has not failed uniquely; the placement has failed, by letting a precise, large-blast-radius output cross the line without a human’s decision attached. Tessera’s reputation, and a week of the customer-success team’s attention, is the blast radius.
The provocation, on the desk of everyone who built it: if this digest ships every Monday and a human only ever approves it, at what point is the human a rubber stamp? The honest answer is the one your working log should capture, and it is not “we review everything.”







Tip🔬 Power-user extension



Core (no-code). Build the digest yourself from the skills-folder idea: three short markdown files — a ticket-clusterer, a knowledge-searcher, a brief-drafter — dropped into an Open WebUI skills folder, with one model pointed at Tessera’s support-tickets and knowledge folders. Run the plan-retrieve-draft loop, then place your checkpoint between search and draft.
Power-user. Take it further one of two ways. Add a real tool-calling step: give the knowledge-searcher a retrieval tool over the knowledge folder and require it to return the source filename and a verbatim quote with every claim — the citation check the case box enforces by hand, now done inside the loop. Or instrument the loop: log, at each step, whether the retrieved source actually contains the phrase the drafter went on to quote, so drift becomes a number you can watch compound instead of a surprise in the finished brief.

section: 10.8 Where this leaves you
text:
10.8 Where this leaves you
An agent is the harness you already understand, extended to act. Its power is real, and so is its danger, and both live in the same place: the tool list, and the loop that calls it. The discipline this chapter adds to prove, don’t persuade is specific. State, before you switch the loop on, every action the agent can take. Name which steps are red-quadrant. Place a checkpoint just before the output becomes load-bearing or irreversible, and be able to defend why there, and not one step later. Treat an agent that could retrieve but didn’t as identical to one that confabulated, because to the reader they are.
Do that and you have answered can it do the whole job? honestly: it can do a great deal of it, fast, and cheaply, and the part it cannot do is the part where someone decides whether what it did is true. That part is yours, and it is not going anywhere.
But there is a question underneath this one we have not yet opened. You have built agents that act, classifiers that sort, models that recommend, and you have treated the model itself as a fixed, opaque thing you point a harness at. How does it actually decide? What is happening inside the weights before the first token ever reaches a chat interface? The next chapter opens the box (quantisation, jagged intelligence, model collapse, and NotebookLM as production-grade RAG to take apart) because you cannot fully prove a system works until you have some handle on what it is doing when it is not being watched.

title: 11  How does it decide?
text:
11.1 The decision inside the box
The chatbot you talk to is a (very large) neural network. Say that sentence slowly, because it does two things at once. It demotes the chatbot from magic to mechanism, a thing with parts you could, in principle, point at. And it reveals that the neural network is just one family of model, sitting beside two older, plainer cousins you have already met in Orange. This is the chapter where you stop asking what does the model say? and start asking how does it decide?, because the second question is the one a CEO will ask you before signing the cheque.
Tessera’s churn problem is the test bed. You will open three models on the same customer data, watch them decide differently, and discover that the most accurate model is rarely the one you can defend. Then you will turn to NotebookLM (Google’s polished retrieval system) and ask the harder question: now that you have built the rough version by hand, can you read the polished one underneath?
Before there was ever a chat interface, the same decide-and-predict mechanics ran in three classic forms. They share one loop:
The four steps are identical for every model you will build this week. The only thing that differs is step two: how it fits.
A logistic regression learns a weight for each input (a positive weight for short tenure, a negative weight for high satisfaction), adds them up, and squashes the total into a probability of churn. The beauty is that the weights are readable. You can point at a coefficient and say “this is the single biggest churn driver the model found.” The limit is that it only captures straight-line, linear relationships.
A decision tree learns a chain of yes/no questions: tenure under six months? a recent complaint? predict churn. You can trace any single prediction down the branches, and explain it to a stakeholder in plain English. A random forest is just many trees voting, which trades a little readability for a lot of sturdiness. A single tree’s weakness is that it can overfit, memorising the training data instead of learning the pattern.
A neural network is layers of artificial neurons, every connection weighted, trained by nudging the weights to reduce error over many passes. It is far more flexible (it can capture patterns the other two cannot) at the cost of being nearly impossible to explain. This is the family the chatbot belongs to, scaled up until the individual decisions disappear into billions of weights.
There is no free lunch. The table tells the whole story:
A model that is easy to explain is often less flexible; a model that is very flexible is hard to explain. In business, the interpretability column is frequently the one that matters, because a model you cannot explain is a model you cannot defend to a stakeholder, or to a regulator. When the decision touches money, the question is rarely “which is smartest?” It is “which can I justify?”

Predict on the test set, the data it has never seen.

You split seventy-thirty, build all three models from the same split, and read each against the same held-out test set.
Then you open each one up. The logistic regression’s coefficients name the biggest churn driver in plain numbers; short tenure and low satisfaction light up, and a region segment stands out: the South and Metro territories churn at roughly two to three times the rate of Central, East, or North. The tree hands you a flowchart you could walk Henrik, Tessera’s CEO, down in a board meeting: fewer than ~6 satisfaction, under ~12 months tenure → churn. The neural network shows you nothing you can read. That opacity is the trade-off made concrete: the most flexible model is the one you cannot defend.
The second artefact is NotebookLM, fed the same Tessera document folder your Chapter 10 agent retrieved from. You are not using it; you are reading it, reverse-engineering the seven-step pipeline underneath against the rough retrieval you built by hand.

title: 11  How does it decide?
section: 11.2 The honest question the data does not answer
text:
11.2 The honest question the data does not answer
Three models, three confusion matrices, and one question the data will never answer for you: for Tessera’s churn problem, which error is worse? Predicting churn for a customer who stays means a wasted retention call (cheap, slightly annoying). Missing a customer who leaves means lost revenue you might have prevented. There is no universal answer. The business call shapes which model “wins.” A model with marginally lower accuracy that catches the real churners may be the better model for this decision, even though it looks worse on a leaderboard.
This is the chapter’s first proof of the spine: accuracy is an assertion, not evidence of fitness. A model that is 84% accurate on average can still miss every customer in the segment that actually matters. The figure on the dashboard persuades; the confusion matrix, read against the business’s real cost of each error, is what proves.






Note🤖 Conversation Log



You ask an AI assistant to help pick a model for Tessera’s churn problem. It replies, confidently and quickly, with a recommendation: the neural network, highest accuracy at 84%. It even drafts a paragraph for the board paper.
This is where you push back, because the AI is optimising the wrong objective. You name two things it did not weigh. First, the direction of the error matters more than its size: missing a churner costs more than a wasted retention call, so recall on the at-risk class is the metric to watch, not raw accuracy. Second, Henrik has to defend the retention budget to the board: the coefficients or the tree let him do that; the neural network does not. The AI was treating accuracy as the goal, when the goal is a defensible, explainable churn decision.
You redirect it: rerun the comparison, weight recall and interpretability, and re-rank. The tree (or the logistic regression) becomes the better model for this decision, at slightly lower accuracy. The lesson lands: an AI will optimise whatever metric you name. Naming the right metric is a business judgement, and that judgement is yours, not the model’s. The machine proposes; you decide what counts as winning.

title: 11  How does it decide?
section: 11.3 A 4-bit model that wins on your task
text:
11.3 A 4-bit model that wins on your task
You have been running a 4-bit quantised Qwen locally since Chapter 5. Quantisation means the model’s weights have been compressed, stored in four bits instead of the usual sixteen. You trade a sliver of precision for a large drop in memory and a real gain in speed. On a laptop, that is the difference between won’t run and runs fine.
Here is the counterintuitive part: a 4-bit local model can outperform a much larger cloud model on a specific task. Not because it is smarter (it is not) but because on a narrow, well-scoped job it can be faster (no network round-trip, no token-billing throttle), private (the data never leaves the machine, the Chapter 6 sovereignty argument), cheap to specialise on your domain, and free at the margin so you can run the loop a thousand times. The lesson is not local beats cloud. It is capability is task-relative. You pick the model that fits the task and its constraints, and that judgement is yours to make and defend, not the vendor’s to sell you.
This pairs with an uncomfortable property of models: they are not uniformly good. They are brilliant at some things and shockingly bad at adjacent things: write flawless code in one language and fumble a near-identical task in another, ace a reasoning puzzle and fail the same puzzle with the numbers swapped. This jaggedness is why the trust tool asks about the task, not the model: a model’s reputation on average tells you almost nothing about its reliability on the specific claim you are about to act on. The only honest answer is to evaluate on your task, on your data, which is exactly what the three-model comparison forces you to do.

title: 11  How does it decide?
section: 11.4 When the data eats itself
text:
11.4 When the data eats itself
There is a slower failure hiding in all of this. When models are trained on text produced by other models, quality can degrade over generations: a slow blurring toward the average, where the rare but real cases quietly disappear. This is model collapse, and it matters now because the open web is filling with model-generated text. The risk for a business is specific: a model trained on contaminated synthetic data loses the long tail, exactly the unusual cases that churn analysis or fraud detection most need to catch. The churner who does not look like the average churner is the one you most need to keep, and the one collapse erases first.
The defence is unglamorous and load-bearing: know where your training and retrieval data came from. Ground in human-authored, domain-specific documents (like the Tessera folder) rather than assuming that more data is always better. Provenance is a feature, not a chore.

title: 11  How does it decide?
section: 11.5 The polished black box you can now read
text:
11.5 The polished black box you can now read
The second half of this chapter turns to a system that hides all of this machinery behind a clean interface: NotebookLM, Google’s production-grade retrieval system. You feed it the Tessera document folder, ask a real question (which region is churning most, and what do the documents suggest is driving it?) and it answers, grounding each claim in a specific source it cites.
The temptation is to be impressed and move on. The discipline is to ask what they built underneath that you built by hand across Chapters 7 and 10. You already know the answer, because you built the rough version: ingest → chunk → embed → retrieve → rank → generate → cite. NotebookLM chunks the documents sensibly, ranks which chunk matters for the question, cites a source per claim, and handles the case where nothing matches. Your rough retrieval did one folder and one lookup; the polished one does all seven steps well, in the dark, where you cannot see them.
This is the point of meeting the polished version after building the rough one. Layer 3 is convenient because it is a black box, and that is exactly why you needed the plain-text and configured layers first. You can trust NotebookLM’s retrieval more because you know what retrieval is, not less. The harness is a black box you can now read, because you once built its guts yourself.






Tip📍 Trust-tool placement



Two outputs, two placements, and a transparency gap between them.
The churn prediction that a retention budget is spent on is precise (a specific flag acted on) with large consequences (money, a customer relationship). That is the red quadrant: a human signs off, no exceptions. The Orange models’ transparency helps (you can show Henrik the coefficient or the branch), but it does not remove the obligation. The decision still crosses a human desk.
NotebookLM’s answer on which region is churning is average-acceptable for the framing, but precise wherever it cites a figure or a document, so yellow: trust the framing, verify the load-bearing citations against their sources. Note the asymmetry. Orange shows you how it decided; NotebookLM hides the retrieval that fed its answer. Both demand placement on the grid. Neither earns trust by default, not even the shiny one.

title: 11  How does it decide?
section: 11.6 What you can now defend
text:
11.6 What you can now defend
You came in asking how does it decide? You leave able to answer it three ways: by reading the weights, by tracing the tree, or by admitting you cannot read the network at all, and choosing accordingly. You know that capability is task-relative, that a smaller local model can win on a narrow job, that models are jagged and must be evaluated on your terms, and that data provenance is the quiet defence against collapse. And you can read a production retrieval system for what it is, because you built its rough ancestor.
This is the practitioner’s moat made concrete. The machine produces the model. You supply the judgement about which model to trust, on which task, with how much oversight, and the evidence to defend it. But a harder question is now unavoidable. If a smaller local model can win on a specific task, and the defensible advantage is shifting from the model to the data and harness around it, then what is the human’s role in choosing and defending a model, and is that role stable? That is the question the final chapter turns to.






Tip🔬 Power-user extension



The Core path is the NotebookLM deconstruction in the case box: build a side-by-side comparison table — your rough hand-rolled RAG against NotebookLM’s polished retrieval — with one row per pipeline stage (ingest, chunk, embed, retrieve, rank, generate, cite) and a note on which stage each system performs visibly versus in the dark. That table alone shows you what you are paying Google for. Doing only this is complete and correct.
To go further, run the same discipline on the Orange side. Re-open the three churn models and read them properly: the ROC curve and AUC in Test & Score tell you how cleanly the classes separate; the confusion matrix widget shows the direction of the errors, which matters more than headline accuracy (as the conversation log showed). Then tune one hyperparameter — the tree’s minimum instances in leaves, or the logistic regression’s regularisation strength — and watch the bias–variance trade-off move in real time: the tree memorises, then blurs; AUC rises, then falls. Sketch the full ingest → chunk → embed → retrieve → rank → generate → cite pipeline on a whiteboard while you do, and you will see both systems — yours and NotebookLM’s — as the same machine, built to different tolerances.

title: 12  What comes next?
text:
12.1 The efficiency story every pitch tells
You are standing in front of Tessera’s leadership team. Henrik Larsson, the CEO, wants to know where the data says to invest. Grace Sullivan, the COO, wants cost-to-serve down without quality dropping. Adrian Vasquez, the CIO, wants to know what is buildable and what is vendor lock-in. And in the room, whether the leadership frames it that way or not, is the support engineer whose task-mix your solution is about to change.
This is where twelve chapters land. Every concept in this book (the trust tool, the harness, the three-lens rubric, the good-enough threshold, the human-in-the-loop) collapses into one artefact: a pitch that does not merely demo, but proves. And every concept the book has quietly been rehearsing (that the human role is to shape how AI lands, not be landed on) is what the decision will rest on.
The pitch is also where the book’s hardest question becomes unavoidable: what comes next? Not as a prediction. As a practice.
Here is the line almost every AI pitch arrives at, sooner or later: “AI makes the work cheaper, so we’ll need fewer people doing it.” It is the default mental model in every deployment memo Tessera’s leadership has read. It is also (historically) almost always wrong.
The reason has a name. In 1865, William Stanley Jevons studied coal use in British factories. New steam engines were dramatically more efficient; they burned less coal per unit of work. The obvious prediction was that coal consumption would fall. It rose. Cheaper work meant more work became worth doing, and total coal use climbed. The pattern has repeated every time a key input gets cheaper. LEDs are roughly ten times more efficient than incandescent bulbs, and total lighting energy has gone up, because we now light everything. Transistors are astronomically cheaper than in 1970; we use astronomically more compute, not less. Bandwidth is cheap; we stream 4K all day rather than rationing it.
The general rule: when an input gets cheaper, demand for the activity it enables tends to grow faster than the efficiency saves. Efficiency does not reduce consumption. It relocates and expands it.
Map it onto AI. The input getting cheaper is cognitive work: drafting, summarising, classifying, searching, first-pass analysis. So the Jevons prediction is not “we’ll do today’s work with fewer people.” It is closer to this: the work that was too expensive to do at all (the analyses we never ran, the customers we never followed up, the documents we never summarised, the edge cases we never tested) will now get done. That is the efficiency trap. A business that deploys AI purely as a headcount play optimises for the wrong thing. The real question is not how do we do today’s work with fewer people? but what work becomes worth doing that wasn’t worth doing before, and who does it, and how do we govern it?
The trap has two jaws, and a good pitch names both. The optimistic jaw: a team that believes AI will simply cut costs builds a thin solution, ships it, and is surprised when demand explodes; they planned for less work and got more, faster, with no governance ready. The pessimistic jaw: a team that believes AI will replace whole roles builds for a future that does not arrive on schedule, and demoralises the very people who are now maintaining the system. The practitioner move is to plan for both: assume the volume of cognitively cheap work goes up, and assume the human role changes rather than vanishes. The trust tool is how you decide which slice of that expanded volume needs a human and which does not.

title: 12  What comes next?
text:
🌐 Tessera Case: The capstone pitch, and its second-order effects
Your team’s capstone pitch is a collaborative churn workflow: an Open WebUI retrieval step pulls from the Tessera knowledge folder, an Orange classifier from Chapter 4 scores churn risk, a local Qwen drafts a retention note, and a support engineer signs off before anything reaches a customer. That hand-off (retrieval to model to human) is what makes it a collaborative workflow rather than a chatbot.
Where the pitch earns trust is the second-order analysis built on top. The cheap version says “this flags churn risk five times faster.” The version the decision rewards runs all four legs: who benefits (HQ accounts, whose retention note now goes out same-day); who pays the transition cost (the support engineer mid-career, whose job is now half drafting-notes-for-AI-to-edit); who is left out (the South and Metro territories, and the Small SME customers, whose ticket language and churn patterns the classifier was never trained on — so the same solution silently underperforms, visible in tessera-support-data.csv); and what Jevons predicts (tier-1 proactive outreach to the 40% of customers currently left on hold, which expands the work rather than shrinking it).
The artefact you hand the decision-makers is not the demo. It is the demo plus the honest second-order sentence: this is worth building, and here is what it costs the people and systems it touches.

title: 12  What comes next?
section: 12.2 Tasks, not jobs
text:
12.2 Tasks, not jobs
So who does the work, once AI has made part of it cheap? The headline question (will AI take our jobs?) is the wrong shape. It treats jobs as fixed buckets that either exist or don’t, and it treats AI as a single event rather than a rolling change. It also has a terrible track record: every wave of automation since the Luddites has been debated in those terms, and the outcome has always been more punctuated and more uneven than either side claimed.
A job is a bundle of tasks. AI rarely replaces a whole job; it changes the mix of tasks inside it. The useful unit of analysis is the task, not the role.
Take a Tessera support engineer. The job bundles reading a ticket, reproducing the issue, searching internal docs, writing a response, escalating hard cases, mentoring juniors, and being the human a frustrated customer talks to. AI reliably changes the first four: drafting, searching, summarising, first-pass triage. It changes almost nothing about the last three: judgement on a genuinely novel outage, mentoring, and the human in a heated conversation. The role does not disappear; it redistributes. The engineer spends less time on the first four and more on the last three. The management challenge is immediate and concrete: how do you redesign that role, retrain for it, re-measure performance, and re-pay for it, without losing the people who hold the institutional knowledge? That is a question for next quarter, not next decade.






Note🤖 Conversation Log



Stress-testing the second-order analysis. To draft the four second-order answers for the churn pitch, the team asked a frontier model: “For this workflow, who captures the upside, who pays the transition cost, and who is left out?”
The model returned a fluent, confident, and almost entirely generic answer: “Small businesses may be disadvantaged; junior staff may be displaced; the firm and large customers benefit.” Plausible, and useless. It had no purchase on Tessera. It was the AI doing what AIs do when asked a distributional question without evidence: producing the average answer, the one that sounds right in any boardroom.
The correction was the prove-don’t-persuade move, applied to the AI’s own output. The team refused the generic and grounded each group in the data instead: pulled satisfaction by territory from the tickets file, pulled ticket-language distribution to surface the South-and-Metro gap, pulled the support engineer’s actual logged hours to see which tasks the workflow absorbed. “Small businesses” became “Small SME accounts in the South and Metro territories, whose tickets the classifier scores with low confidence.” “Junior staff displaced” became “the two mid-career engineers whose tickets-to-resolutions the workflow now mediates.” The model produced the draft; the team supplied the evidence, and in doing so supplied the one thing the average could not: the specific people this solution touches.
The lesson, at the close of the book, is that the same scepticism you apply to a churn score applies to the AI’s account of who your solution harms. An ungrounded second-order analysis is still an assertion. Ground it, or strike it.

title: 12  What comes next?
section: 12.3 Who pays, who benefits, who is left out
text:
12.3 Who pays, who benefits, who is left out
That last move, naming the specific people, is the one the technology press tends to flatten into “AI is good” or “AI is bad.” The honest version is distributional: the gains and the costs of an AI deployment do not fall on the same people. Three groups, always named.
Who captures the upside? The firm that deploys it, the customer whose service gets faster, the worker whose drudge work shrinks, the vendor selling the model. These are not the same actor, and they do not split the gains evenly. Who pays the transition cost? Almost always the worker whose task-mix changes mid-career, the team that has to maintain a system that “works,” and the customer whose problem was an edge case the model was never trained on. Who is left out entirely? The people the solution was never built for: small customers, non-English speakers, the region with the worst data, the applicant whose résumé the screening model never surfaced. Exclusion is rarely announced; it shows up as silence.
This is not a moral decoration on the analysis. It is the analysis. And you have been living it across the whole book without the label. A careful team runs a local Qwen alongside a frontier model on purpose. From Chapter 2 onwards the argument was: a team where some members can afford a frontier subscription and others cannot is not a level playing field. Local AI is an equity decision before it is a technical one. That is the political economy of AI in miniature. Scale it up: which organisations can afford to deploy frontier AI, and which get the local or open version? Which regions have the infrastructure, and which don’t? Which workforces get retrained, and which get “disrupted”? The same question that decided whether you ran Qwen locally or paid for a subscription decides who in the economy gets to participate in the AI layer at all.
A practitioner who cannot name these groups is not a practitioner; they are a deployer. This book’s job is to produce the former. Your pitch is judged, in part, on whether you can hold the upside and the cost in the same sentence.






Tip📍 Trust-tool placement



Where the pitch’s outputs sit on the grid. Place the capstone artefact one piece at a time. The live demo slice (a ranked churn list, a drafted retention note) is 🟡 yellow: average is fine on the framing, but the load-bearing claim (which customer is actually at risk) must be precise, so a human verifies it before it drives an action. The retention note itself, if it goes to a customer, is 🔴 red: large blast radius, precise requirement, human signs off, non-negotiable. The trust-tool checkpoint is not a flourish in the pitch; it is the design.
And then the pitch’s second-order analysis (the who benefits, who pays, who is left out) is itself a 🔴 red-quadrant output, and here is the irony worth noticing. The demo slice looks like the load-bearing part, so teams spend the rehearsal polishing it. But the decision the leadership makes (build this, or don’t) rests on the second-order claims, not the demo. Treating those claims as green (skim and trust) is the failure mode this book has spent twelve chapters trying to dislodge. The placement instinct, one last time: the thing that looks like decoration is often the thing that is load-bearing.

title: 12  What comes next?
section: 12.4 Planning for a range
text:
12.4 Planning for a range
And then there is the trajectory. There is a cottage industry in predicting when artificial general intelligence arrives. The dates range from “it’s already here” to “never,” and the people making the predictions have been wrong, in both directions, for sixty years. This chapter is not about joining that industry. There is a different, more useful discipline: planning assumptions.
A prediction is a claim about what will happen. A planning assumption is a stance about what you do given that you don’t know. Practitioners live in the second register. You do not get to wait for the forecast to settle before you build, hire, or govern. For planning purposes, the philosophical definition of AGI matters less than the capability trajectory: models keep getting better at a widening set of economically useful tasks, the cost per unit of cognitive work keeps falling, and the rate of both has repeatedly surprised people who expected a plateau. You felt this trajectory in the book itself. In Chapter 1 you ran the same prompt on a local Qwen and a frontier model and saw the gap. By Chapter 10 you were wiring that same local model into a multi-step agentic loop. The gap between what a free local model can do and what a frontier model can do is not fixed; it moves. That movement is the planning assumption.
There are three stances, and only two survive contact with reality. Plan for stasis: assume the capability you deploy today is the capability you will have. Comforting, and almost always wrong; systems designed around one model’s quirks break when the model improves, and prompts that exploit a weakness stop working when the weakness is patched. Plan for a specific date: assume “AGI by 20XX” and build for that. This is a prediction dressed as a plan; be wrong by two years and you have built too early or too late, and spent the political capital of being a doomer or a laggard. Plan for a range: assume capability improves along a corridor, design so the system stays useful and safe across that corridor, and re-baseline regularly. This is the only durable stance. It treats the trajectory as a weather system you sail through, not a wall you hit.
Stance three has practical teeth. It means build harnesses, not prompts. Keep the trust-tool placement current rather than fixed. Prefer solutions that degrade gracefully when the model changes. And put the human-in-the-loop controls in now, while it is cheap, not after a model upgrade removes the option quietly.
Look back. Every chapter has been a small rehearsal of stance three. The local-vs-frontier comparison taught you to judge outputs, not brands, so your judgement survives a model swap. The harness as plain text taught you a portable skill that does not expire when a vendor changes pricing. The trust tool, every chapter, taught you to re-place outputs on the grid as capability shifts, instead of trusting “the good model” by default. The conversation log taught you to document your own thinking, which is the one thing that does not depreciate as models improve.

title: 12  What comes next?
section: 12.5 The question is now yours
text:
12.5 The question is now yours
Here is the honest answer to the book’s secondary thread: if AI keeps getting better, what is the human role, and is it stable? It is not a doomer question. It is the planning question. The human role is to do the things stance three requires: place outputs on the grid, design the harness, hold the governance, name who is left out, and re-baseline when the ground moves. That role is not stable in its tasks. It is stable in its function. Whether it stays stable is genuinely open. You are now equipped to hold the question without pretending to answer it.
Twelve chapters ago, the demo and the deployment were the same thing to you: something that looked impressive, that you would build and trust. Now they are not. A demo is engineered to persuade. A deployment has to actually work: survive the inputs the demo never showed you, fail gracefully where it must, and be trusted, or not, by the people who depend on it. The discipline that closes that gap has a name. Prove, don’t persuade. Every claim about an AI solution is an assertion until evidence supports it. The model produces the draft; you supply the judgement, the evidence, and the defensible conclusion.
In a world of demos, the proof is the point. The machine will keep getting better at building the demo; that is the trajectory you now plan against, not bet on. Your edge is the discipline that turns a demo into something a business can actually ship, with the right oversight, for the right people, honestly named where it fails. The question (what comes next?) is now genuinely yours to hold. So is the proof.






Tip🔬 Power-user extension



Ground each leg of the second-order pitch in measured evidence. The Core — the no-code path everyone completes — is to assemble the capstone pitch with its four legs named. The Power-user move is to make each leg a number, not an adjective. Three concrete asks:

Disaggregated accuracy. In Orange, use Select Rows to filter the churn data to one segment at a time (say Region = South, then Company_Size = Small), feed each subset through the trained classifier, and read the per-group accuracy from the Confusion Matrix. The overall accuracy can look fine while the model silently underperforms on the South and Metro territories and on Small SME accounts — the exact left-out leg of the pitch. Quote the worst-group gap.
Transition cost on a sample. Pull ten real tickets from tessera-support-data.csv and time the before/after task-mix for the mid-career engineer: how many minutes now go to drafting-notes-for-AI-to-edit. A measured cost on a sample beats an asserted cost every time.
Name the left-out segment with data. From tessera-customer-data.csv, count the customers in the segments the classifier was never trained on (Small × South, Small × Metro). Naming 43 specific customers rather than a generic some-customers hand-wave is what turns the equity leg from decoration into evidence.

title: A. The Trust Tool
text:
The two questions
The trust tool is the one idea this book uses in every chapter. It is small enough to fit on a sticky note and general enough to survive any model swap. Before you act on any AI output, you place it on a grid by answering two questions, and the grid tells you what to do next: skim it, check the load-bearing bit, or send it through a human before it touches anything real.
Almost every public AI failure is a placement failure. The chatbot that gave wrong legal advice, the hallucinated citation in a filed court document, the churn flag nobody checked: each is someone treating a red-quadrant output as green. The model rarely fails uniquely. The placement fails, because nobody made it a conscious act. This appendix is the tool in full.
Answer the two and you have a coordinate on the grid.

title: A. The Trust Tool
text:
Does this output need to be precise, or is average fine?

Average means roughly right is good enough: a brainstorm, a first draft, a summary that points you where to look. If it is a little off, the cost is small.
Precise means the answer has to be right, because someone or something will act on it: a customer gets called, a contract clause gets relied on, a fault gets cleared.

If it is wrong, how big is the blast radius, small or large?

Small means a mistake costs a glance or a re-do: a misrouted ticket, a clumsy sentence.
Large means a mistake lands on a real person, a real budget, or a real decision: a churn prediction, a hiring screen, a support reply a customer reads.

title: A. The Trust Tool
section: What each placement tells you to do
text:
What each placement tells you to do

🟢 Green, skim and use. The output is roughly right and the cost of being wrong is small. Read it, use it, move on. Drafts, brainstorms, document pulls, triage of low-stakes tickets.
🟡 Yellow, verify the load-bearing bit. Most of the output can stand, but one claim carries the weight, and that is the claim you check. A strategic framing, a retrieved answer with a source, a summary that feeds a decision. Find the sentence a decision would rest on, and confirm it.
🔴 Red, a human signs off before it touches anything real. The output must be right and a mistake lands on a person. A churn flag acted on, a customer reply sent, a fault cleared, a hire screened. Human-in-the-loop, non-negotiable, and the model said so is never a defence.

title: A. The Trust Tool
section: How to place well
text:
How to place well
The tool is a discipline, not a formula. These are the moves the chapters rehearse.
Place before you act. Placement is a conscious step before you ship, because the surface will never warn you. A fluent, polished output is exactly the one nobody checks, and that is the danger.
Judge outputs, not models. A frontier model and a local four-bit Qwen can each produce green-quadrant brilliance and red-quadrant garbage on the same afternoon. You are learning to judge the output in front of you, not the brand on the box. Your judgement has to survive a model swap, because the swap is coming.
The same screen can hold two placements. One output can flip quadrant mid-sentence. A brainstorm of candidate churn drivers is green; the instant a specific customer count and revenue figure appears, the same screen is red. A segment description (“Basic-tier customers churn at roughly three times the base rate”) is green; a per-customer score (“flag customer C0xxx for a save call”) is red. Read each claim, not each screen.
Fluency raises the stakes. A confident, well-structured output disarms scrutiny. The better the prose, the less likely anyone checks, so the more disciplined your placement has to be. Confidence is a delivery property, not a truth property.
Anything that touches a person is red until a human has checked it. A churn flag, a customer persona, a screening ranking, a support reply: each lands on a real person, so each is red regardless of how polished it looks. This is the rule that runs under every chapter.
Place per step, not per workflow. The moment you give a model tools and let it act (an agent), placement becomes a decision per step. Clustering might be yellow, retrieval green, the final brief red. Put your checkpoint just before the step that becomes load-bearing or irreversible, and be able to defend why there, and not one step later.
Controls move red toward yellow; they do not retire your judgement. Good architecture, privacy-by-design, a sourced retrieval step: these shrink the blast radius or make the claim checkable. They move a red output to yellow (“verify the load-bearing bits before sending”). They do not promote it to green. A human still reads it.
Re-place as capability shifts. A model that scores 0% on faults this year might creep to 99% next year, and a red square could move to yellow. But only a fresh evaluation moves it, not hope, and not the vendor’s demo. Re-place on evidence, on a schedule.

title: A. The Trust Tool
section: When yellow or red: the four lenses
text:
When yellow or red: the four lenses
When a placement tells you to verify, Chapter 3’s four lenses turn “check it” into something you can actually do. For each lens, write one sentence of evidence pulled from the actual output, not a vibe.

Representativeness: who is in the data or output? Who is missing or thinly drawn?
Harm: if this output drove a decision, who could be disadvantaged, and would they know?
Accountability: who is responsible if it is wrong? Can they be identified and reached?
Transparency: can you see how it produced the answer, and show someone else?

Representativeness and Harm tell you the blast radius. Accountability and Transparency tell you whether a human is genuinely in the loop. Fail either pair and the output stays red until it is fixed, not shipped. “It seems a bit biased” is not evidence; “the at-risk profile defaults to one industry and company size, which excludes every customer in the South and Metro territories” is.

title: A. The Trust Tool
section: The two mistakes to avoid
text:
The two mistakes to avoid
Treating red as green is the failure mode this book exists to catch. It is rarely malicious; it is the natural drift of a polished output nobody made themselves place.
Blobbing a workflow into one cell is the agent-era version of the same mistake. An agent is a chain of outputs, each with its own failure surface. One placement for the whole chain means the red step slips through unnamed. Place per step; checkpoint the red ones.






Note



The trust tool comes from the companion book, Conversation, Not Delegation, which teaches it as part of the conversation loop. This appendix is the same tool through the lens of this book: applied AI, where placement is the act that turns a demo into something you can defend.

title: B. The Conversation Log Format
text:
Why it exists
A conversation log is the artefact that makes your thinking with AI visible. It is the cumulative record you keep across the book: what you asked, how you pushed back, what you verified, and what you decided to trust. Each chapter’s Conversation Log feature is the book version of the same discipline. This appendix is the format in full, so you can keep one of your own.
The log is where prove, don’t persuade stops being a slogan and becomes a habit. A demo persuades; a log proves, because it shows the work, including the parts where the AI was confidently wrong and you caught it.
An AI session that goes smoothly proves nothing. If the model agreed with you the whole way and you shipped its answer, you have a transcript of agreement, and agreement is not evidence. The value of a conversation log is in the corrections: the moment the model drifted, the claim it smoothed over, the figure it invented, and the specific pushback that put it back on the rails. That is where your judgement becomes visible, and it is the part that shows whether the work is yours.
A good log also keeps you honest about the trust tool. Every entry forces you to place the output before you act, and to say, in writing, which load-bearing bit you verified and why. Over twelve chapters that repetition turns placement into a reflex.

title: B. The Conversation Log Format
section: The entry
text:
The entry
One entry per substantive session. Keep it short enough to read in a minute; attach the raw transcript for the detail.

Date, model(s), and goal. What were you trying to figure out, and which model(s) did you use? Name the model, because a finding that holds for a frontier model and a local Qwen is worth more than one that holds for a single brand.
Trust-tool placement. Average or precise? Small or large blast radius? Which traffic light, and what does it tell you to verify? State this before you write the conclusion, not after.
The prompts that mattered. The turning points, not the whole chat. If you used the RTCF frame (Role, Task, Context, Format), say so and quote the prompt that changed the session. Three to five prompts is usually enough.
Where the AI was wrong, and how you corrected it. The load-bearing part. Quote the model’s wrong claim, name why it was wrong (the split it misread, the constraint it dropped, the average it hid behind), and show the pushback. This is what the log is for.
What you decided to trust, and why. One or two lines you would act on, and the evidence that earns the trust. “The satisfaction-and-tenure story is robust enough to act on lightly; the segment spike is a question, not a lever; the sparse-cell pattern I discarded.” The defensible answer, not the fluent one.
Full transcript. Saved unedited, as an appendix to the entry or a linked file. You never edit the transcript, because the unedited record is the integrity gate. If you are tempted to tidy the model’s embarrassing error, that error is exactly what the reader needs to see.

title: B. The Conversation Log Format
section: What a good entry does (and doesn’t)
text:
What a good entry does (and doesn’t)
A good entry shows the friction. It records the disagreement that produced the insight, places the output honestly, and ends on a defensible line with its evidence named.
A good entry does not log only the agreements, edit the transcript, hide the model’s errors, or present the AI’s fluent first draft as the conclusion. If your log reads as a smooth collaboration where the AI was right every time, you have written persuasion, not proof, and you have missed the point of the book.

title: B. The Conversation Log Format
section: A worked shape
text:
A worked shape
The Conversation Log features in Chapters 1 to 12 all follow this shape. The Chapter 4 log is a compact example: the goal (ask an AI partner what Tessera should do with the churn tree), the two errors (reading a correlation as a cause; chasing noise in a sparse segment cell), the corrections (the satisfaction/tenure split is correlation not cause; the small-cell spread is overfitting), and the defensible conclusion (act lightly on satisfaction and tenure; treat the segment spike as a question; discard the sparse-cell split). Two errors, two corrections, one trusted line. That is the whole pattern, and it is the pattern your working log repeats.

title: B. The Conversation Log Format
section: How it assembles into a body of work
text:
How it assembles into a body of work
The conversation log is the spine of your working record. Across the twelve chapters it accumulates into the evidence that you can work with AI as a thinking partner and still supply the judgement the machine cannot: placing each output, catching each drift, and defending each decision you acted on. A reader who reads only your logs should be able to tell, for every artefact you built, which claim you trusted, which you verified, and which you refused. That is what prove, don’t persuade looks like on paper.






Note



The conversation log is taught in full in the companion book, Conversation, Not Delegation, as part of the conversation loop. This appendix is the same format through the lens of this book: the cumulative record that turns an applied-AI build into something a human can stand behind.

title: C. What You Build
text:
The artefacts, by chapter
This appendix is the inventory of what you produce across the twelve chapters: the artefacts, the tools, where each sits on the trust grid, and what each one proved. Not every chapter produces a thing you would call a build. Some produce an audit, a decision, or a proof. They are all here, because each is an artefact you can point to, defend, and place in your body of work.
The pattern underneath them is the one this book keeps returning to. The machine can produce the demo for any of them in an afternoon. The thing that is yours, and the thing you must be able to defend, is the proof: the placement, the evaluation, the correction, and the defensible line you would act on.

title: C. What You Build
section: Two things run through all of them
text:
Two things run through all of them
Every artefact above carries the same two companions, and together they are what turn a build into something defensible.

The trust tool (Appendix A) places each artefact before you act on it. Several sit in two cells at once (green and red a line apart), and the placement is the act that stops the red one slipping through as green.
The conversation log (Appendix B) records the thinking that produced each artefact, including where the AI was wrong and how you corrected it. It is the evidence the artefact was proved, not persuaded.

title: C. What You Build
section: How it assembles into a body of work
text:
How it assembles into a body of work
Your body of work has two halves, and this appendix is the spine of the first.

The build. The artefacts in the table above, each with its evaluation and its placement. A reader should be able to take any one of them and see what it does, where it fails, and how much oversight it needs.
The thinking. The conversation logs (Appendix B) that produced them, showing the pushback and the corrections.
The capstone (Chapter 12). The pitch that synthesises the whole engagement against Tessera, including the second-order analysis the decision actually rests on.

The moat was never in building these. A chatbot can produce most of them in minutes. The moat is in reading each one correctly: placing it, evaluating it, catching where it is generic or wrong, and defending the decision you made about it. That is what prove, don’t persuade looks like as a body of work.

title: D. From Prototype to Production
text:
The honest boundary
Every artefact in Appendix C is, at the moment you finish it, a working prototype. It runs. It passed the evaluation you designed for it. You placed it on the trust grid and named its limits. That is a long way from a demo, and it is still not the same thing as a system a business can rely on, live, with its reputation on the line.
This appendix is about the gap between proved it works and keeps working in production. It is the layer the twelve chapters point at but do not build out, because it belongs to the operational lifetime of a system, not to the act of building one. The thesis does not change: prove, don’t persuade. It just does not stop at launch.
The no-code tools in this book (Orange, Open WebUI, Teachable Machine, an agent framework) will get you to a deployable prototype: something that works, that you have evaluated honestly, and that you can defend. They will not, on their own, run a hardened production system. Production is where software engineering begins: monitoring, rollback, access control, incident response, scaling, cost management.
Knowing where that line sits is itself the practitioner’s edge. The dangerous practitioner is the one who ships a polished prototype as if it were a production system, because they cannot see the line. The useful practitioner can say, for any artefact: this far I can build, evaluate, and defend; from here, engineering and operations take it, and here is exactly what they must not drop. This appendix is a map of that handoff, not a course in it.

title: D. From Prototype to Production
section: What changes when you go live
text:
What changes when you go live
A prototype has to run. A production system has to do four things a prototype never did.
It has to keep working. The model that scored well in your evaluation is not frozen. The world drifts: customers behave differently, the input distribution shifts, a vendor swaps the model under your API. An accuracy figure measured once is a photograph, not a guarantee. The question stops being does it work? and becomes is it still working, and how would I know if it stopped?
It has to fail visibly. A prototype fails on your laptop, where you see it. A production system fails in front of customers, quietly, and the worst failure is the one nobody notices until a complaint arrives. You need telemetry that surfaces the failure, not a dashboard of green ticks that hides it. Chapter 3’s lesson scales up: the dangerous output is the fluent one nobody checked, and the dangerous system is the one whose failures are invisible to the team that owns it.
Someone has to own it. A prototype is yours. A production system needs an owner, an on-call, and a named human who signs off on the red-quadrant outputs. “The model does this” is not an operating model; it is the shadow system from Chapter 3, now running in production. Name the owner before you ship, or the ownership defaults to nobody.
The legal and security questions become gates. In a prototype, the Privacy Act questions (Chapter 6) and the injection defences (Chapter 3) are things you considered. In production they are gates a launch does not pass without: data-processing agreements in place, cross-border transfers lawful for the regions you serve, least-privilege tooling on any agent, and a human approval step on every action that is hard to reverse. Chapter 5 chose where the prompt may travel; production makes that choice auditable and enforced.

title: D. From Prototype to Production
section: A production checklist (for a no-code practitioner)
text:
A production checklist (for a no-code practitioner)
This is what to demand of any system you move from proved prototype to live, phrased for someone who will hand it to engineers rather than build the engineering themselves.

Watch the metric you evaluated on, sliced the way you evaluated it. Not aggregate accuracy. The per-class, per-segment, per-condition view is what caught the fault class collapsing under dim light (Chapter 9). In production that view is your canary; the aggregate is the lie that hid the failure in the first place.
Re-evaluate on a schedule and on every change. A model swap, a new data source, a prompt rewrite: each is a reason to re-run the evaluation and re-place the output on the grid. Appendix A’s rule holds: re-place on evidence, on a schedule, never on hope.
Have a kill switch, and know who can pull it. If the system cannot be turned off fast, it is not production-ready. Name the person, the channel, and the threshold at which they act.
Make the human-in-the-loop a design, not a promise. A checkpoint that survives Monday-morning volume and deadline pressure is the only one that counts. The Delegation Trap (Chapter 3) does not disappear at launch; it intensifies, because production volume is exactly the pressure that turns a reviewer into a rubber stamp. Design the checkpoint so that rubber-stamping is hard, not easy.
Log for audit, not for curiosity. Keep the records that let you answer, after a complaint, what did the system do, why, and who decided to trust it. The conversation log (Appendix B) is the prototype version of this discipline; production makes it a requirement.
Sign off at go-live, on paper. The deployment decision (Chapter 5), the privacy architecture (Chapter 6), the security baseline (Chapter 3): each needs a named sign-off before launch, not a nod. A launch memo that records what was checked, by whom, and what the known limits are, is the artefact that separates a responsible deployment from a hopeful one.

title: D. From Prototype to Production
section: Worked example: the router classifier, live
text:
Worked example: the router classifier, live
Take the Chapter 9 classifier to production. The evaluation already did the hard part: it found the fault class collapses to 0% under dim light, and you placed fault confirmation as red (a human verifies) and triage as green. Production does not re-litigate that; it operationalises it.

Monitoring: track the fault-detection rate and the false-clear rate over time, sliced by lighting condition, because dim-light faults are exactly where this model breaks.
Re-evaluation: re-run the held-out evaluation whenever the fleet gets a new LED design, a firmware update, or a new product line, because any of those shifts the input distribution the model was trained on.
Checkpoint: the human-verify-fault step is the load-bearing control. It must survive the volume of real tickets, which means it has to be fast and specific (show the human the photo and the model’s call, ask one question), not a generic “please review.”
Kill switch: if the false-clear rate climbs past a threshold, auto-clearing of faults stops and everything routes to a human until the model is re-evaluated.

The model did not change between prototype and production. What changed is that the proof became continuous, the oversight became enforced, and the failure that was once caught in an evaluation is now caught by a system that keeps looking for it.

title: D. From Prototype to Production
section: Where this book stops
text:
Where this book stops
This book teaches you to build a prototype that works, evaluate it until it breaks, and defend the decision about how much to trust it. It stops short of teaching you to run it in production, because that is a different discipline, and pretending otherwise would be the demo mindset this book exists to resist.
What it does give you is the ability to see the line, to hand the system over with its limits honestly named, and to specify the oversight that must travel with it. A practitioner who can do that is the one a business trusts to deploy AI. A practitioner who cannot is the one who ships a demo and calls it production, and the cost of the difference lands on the customer, the regulator, and the reputation that was on the line all along.

title: E. The Tessera Case — A Living Example
text:
The company, in one paragraph
Tessera is fictional. It is also, deliberately, real enough to explore. The company, its people, its documents, and its datasets exist as a living companion site at tessera.locoensayo.org. Nothing in this book depends on visiting it — every dataset, document, and decision the chapters use is described in full right here. But if you learn by poking at things, the site turns the case from a thought experiment into an extended reality you can walk around in.
This appendix is the map. Use it to go deeper on any chapter, or ignore it entirely.
Tessera is an Australian managed-cloud and multi-tenant SaaS provider, founded in Perth in 2011, with offices in Sydney and an operations centre in Malaga, Western Australia. It serves more than 600 clients across the SME and enterprise segments and employs around 210 people. Its platform runs on AWS (primary region Sydney, standby Singapore), and it holds ISO/IEC 27001 and SOC 2 Type II certifications. Its stated values are security first, customer success, evidence over assertion — and that last one is the reason it is the right case for a book about proof.

title: E. The Tessera Case — A Living Example
section: Why the breach matters here
text:
Why the breach matters here
Tessera recently lived through an incident it records as TSR-INC-2025-031: a long-lived cloud access key leaked through a misconfigured code repository, and — because the management plane was not properly segmented from the tenant-data plane — that key was used to read tenant data for an estimated five days before anyone noticed. Around 14,000 tenant records were exposed; 23 clients did not renew; the first-year impact was on the order of $1.8 million. The regulator was notified under the Australian Notifiable Data Breaches scheme.
That incident is not the subject of this book. It is the backdrop. It is the reason Tessera’s board now demands evidence rather than assertion for anything that touches customer data — including the AI systems the company is building. A company that has just paid the price of an unverified assumption is exactly the company that needs a practitioner who proves, don’t persuade. Read the breach as the pressure that makes every chapter’s question urgent.

section: Orange Data Mining — visual machine learning
text:
Orange Data Mining — visual machine learning
Orange is a drag-and-drop tool for classical machine learning. You build a workflow by placing widgets on a canvas and wiring them together; each widget is a step you can open and inspect. It is the tool this book uses to make decision trees, clustering, and sentiment visible — literally, because you can see every split.

Get it: https://orangedatamining.com/download. Installers for macOS, Windows, Linux.
First run: open it, drag a File widget onto the canvas, double-click it, and load a CSV. Drag a Data Table and a Distributions widget, wire them to File, and you are looking at data. That is the whole interaction model.
For Chapter 4: File → Decision Tree → Tree Viewer, and File → k-Means for clustering.
No account, no cloud. Your data stays on your machine. That matters in Chapter 6.

title: F. The No-Code Toolkit — Getting Started
section: Google Teachable Machine — train a model in the browser
text:
Google Teachable Machine — train a model in the browser
Teachable Machine lets you train an image, audio, or pose classifier in a browser tab using transfer learning. You point a webcam (or upload images), click Train Model, and export a working model you can put on a web page. It is the most approachable way to experience “I built and shipped a model” in an afternoon — which is exactly why Chapter 9 uses it.

Get it: https://teachablemachine.withgoogle.com. A Google account helps for saving projects; the tool itself is free.
For Chapter 9: create an Image Project, add 2–3 classes, capture ~15–25 images per class varying the conditions on purpose, click Train Model, then Export → TensorFlow.js → “Upload my model”. Drop the link it gives you into the Glitch starter (below) and your classifier is live on your phone.
Glitch starter: remix the Teachable Machine starter at https://glitch.com (search “Teachable Machine”) to turn your exported model into a web app anyone can open.
Power-user note: the same export can be downloaded and self-hosted, which is the sovereignty move from Chapter 5 applied to a model you built.

title: F. The No-Code Toolkit — Getting Started
section: NotebookLM — retrieval, as a black box you can open
text:
NotebookLM — retrieval, as a black box you can open
NotebookLM is Google’s polished retrieval system: you give it a set of source documents and it answers questions about them, with citations. It is, in this book’s terms, a production-grade harness you did not build. Chapter 11 uses it as the thing you deconstruct — you compare it against the rough retrieval you built by hand and ask what they built underneath it.

Get it: https://notebooklm.google.com. A free Google account.
For Chapter 11: create a notebook, add the same document folder you used for your Chapter 7 retrieval, and ask it questions. Then ask the harder question: what did it do (chunking, ranking, citation) that your folder-and-a-sentence version did not?
A reminder from Chapter 11: NotebookLM is here to be read, not just used. The point of meeting it after you built the rough version is that you can see the seams.

title: F. The No-Code Toolkit — Getting Started
section: Ollama — run a model on your own machine
text:
Ollama — run a model on your own machine
Ollama is the engine that runs a large language model locally, on your own hardware, with no data leaving your machine. It is the sovereignty and equity story of Chapter 5 made literal: the same capable model for everyone, free at the margin, private by construction.

Get it: https://ollama.com/download. Install, then in a terminal run ollama run qwen3:8b (or whichever model the chapter names). The first run downloads the model — a few gigabytes, once.
What that tag means: qwen3:8b is an 8-billion-parameter instruction-tuned model, stored 4-bit quantised so it fits in roughly 5 GB and runs on a normal laptop. Chapter 11 explains quantisation; for setup, just know the compression is why it runs on your hardware.
It runs offline once the model is downloaded. No account, no per-query bill, no data sent anywhere.

title: F. The No-Code Toolkit — Getting Started
section: Open WebUI — the chat interface
text:
Open WebUI — the chat interface
Open WebUI is the chat front-end this book uses to point at a model and a knowledge folder. If you have used ChatGPT in a browser, you already know how to use it. The difference is that you choose the model and you control the documents.

Get it: the simplest path is to run it alongside Ollama; see the install instructions at https://github.com/open-webui/open-webui. A shared hosted instance (run by a team or a classroom) lets you skip local install entirely and just point a browser at it.
For Chapter 7: create a knowledge folder, drop in your documents, set a one-line system prompt, and you have built retrieval-augmented generation — the model reads your files before answering.
For Chapter 10: the same folder-plus-model idea extends into a multi-step agent that reads, retrieves, and drafts.

section: A note on equity

A note on equity
The reason this toolkit is all free is not accident or charity. It is the argument Chapter 2 makes in miniature: if the capability to evaluate AI is gated behind a paid subscription, then only the people who can pay get to develop the judgement the field depends on — and the rest get to be deployed on. A no-code floor built on free, offline-capable tools is the cheapest way to put that judgement in everyone’s hands. Install what you need, do the Core, and add the Power-user ceiling only if and when you want it.

title: Acknowledgments
text:
This book grew out of a frustration and an opportunity. The frustration: applied AI is too often taught as build a demo: a classifier that works on the tidy data, a chatbot that answers the easy question, a dashboard of green ticks. Demos persuade. They do not prove anything, and the moment a solution meets real customers, real edge cases, and real blast radii, the demo’s confidence collapses. The opportunity: AI is commoditising the very craft of building those demos, which forces the harder question: what is a human practitioner actually for when a machine can build the prototype? This book is an attempt to answer both at once: to give applied AI a readable, opinionated spine, and to take a clear stance on evidence in a world where the demo is cheap and the proof is the point.
This book began in a classroom — with readers who do not write code learning to build and evaluate applied AI for the first time. Their prototypes that broke in surprising ways, their honesty when a model they trusted failed an entire customer segment, and their moments of “oh, that’s why we evaluate” shaped every chapter. Tessera is written for them, and the discipline this book teaches (prove, don’t persuade) is the one they carry into every solution they build and ship. The book now stands on its own; where its path happens to align with a course, that is a happy coincidence rather than a requirement.
This book sits in a small family, and the family made it better. Conversation, Not Delegation taught the method of working with AI as a thinking partner; Substantiate, Don’t Assume taught the audit sibling of this same instinct. Prove, Don’t Persuade is the build-and-evaluate companion to both. Where those books ask how do we work with the machine? and what do we verify?, this one asks the question that lands on every applied-AI practitioner’s desk: does it actually work, and how do you know?
Colleagues who reviewed early drafts and pushed back on arguments that were not yet strong enough made the book sharper. You know who you are, and I am grateful.
The open-source community behind Quarto, Pandoc, and GitHub made it possible to write, build, and publish this book with tools that are free and transparent. The open tools the book itself teaches (Orange Data Mining, Ollama, Open WebUI, Teachable Machine, and NotebookLM) are what make no-code, equity-first applied AI possible at all. That those tools are free and capable is not a footnote; it is the enabling condition for everything in these pages.
This book was written using the methodology its companion, Conversation, Not Delegation, describes. AI was involved at every stage: as a drafting partner, a sounding board, and, crucially, a source of plausible-sounding mistakes that needed catching. That last role is the point. A practitioner’s relationship to AI-generated work is exactly what this book teaches: the machine produces the draft, and the demo; the human supplies the judgement, the evidence, and the defensible answer to does it actually work? Every sentence here reflects the author’s judgement. The AI made the work faster. It did not do the thinking, and it certainly did not do the proving.

title: About the Author
text:
Photo of Michael Borck


Michael Borck is a software developer and educator working at the intersection of human expertise and artificial intelligence. He teaches applied AI and AI-driven knowledge systems, and the question that started this book (what is a human practitioner actually for when a machine can build the demo?) is the one he asks in every class he runs.
His earlier book, Conversation, Not Delegation, argues that AI is most valuable not as a tool you delegate to, but as a thinking partner you converse with. Prove, Don’t Persuade is the discipline that pairs with that craft: it is about what a practitioner must prove (not persuade, not demo) once the building is done. The two books are companions: one on how to work with the machine, one on how to know the work actually holds up. It has a sibling in Substantiate, Don’t Assume, which teaches the same proof-instinct on the auditor’s desk.
The thesis grew out of a realisation that surfaced again and again in his classroom: a polished AI prototype is easy to produce and almost impossible to trust on its face. The real skill, and the durable one, is evaluation: stating what “good enough” means, measuring honestly, naming who a solution fails, and deciding how much a human must stay in the loop. That skill does not expire when the next model arrives, and it cannot be delegated to the model itself.
Michael builds educational software and resources, and writes about the 80/20 principle in learning and professional judgement.
